articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Xen Orchestra Auth Bypass Flaw to Gain Admin Access
articles.context: French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild
articles.full_text:
French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild.

The authentication bypass flaw, which does not yet have a CVE identifier, is tracked as VSA-2026-062.

"REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}," Vates VMS said in an alert. "REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string."

"The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs."

In other words, the vulnerability can allow an attacker to bypass authentication by sending a specially crafted cookie and perform arbitrary actions with "Admin" privileges, ultimately resulting in arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.

Vates VMS said it's seeing the vulnerability being actively exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain -

91.211.251[.]112:8001, which has been flagged as a RedLine Stealer command-and-control (C2) server on VirusTotal

ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333

It's unclear when the activity started and if the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day.

Other indicators of compromise are listed below -

HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}

A running virtual machine named pivot2

Virtual machines configured using "hvm_serial: file" parameter

Suspicious files named /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6

The issue has been addressed in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 for the stable and latest channels, as well as xo-server versions 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. If immediate patching is not an option, the following mitigations are advised -

Avoid exposing Xen Orchestra instances on the internet

Block the IP address and domain associated with malicious activity

Block the empty token in a web application firewall (WAF) or a reverse proxy

Rotate all passwords and secrets in Vates VMS if indicators of compromise are detected

Filip Magic (@mad31k) and Christoffer Olsen from TDC NET Security have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw.

articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.context: Get an updated version of Git > The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog
articles.full_text:
Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

[Advisory]

Additional hardening

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Protecting GitHub users

We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.

We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.

GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.

Update Git

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Get an updated version of Git >

The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

articles.title: Critical Xen Orchestra auth bypass flaw exploited to hijack VM servers
articles.context: A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng...
articles.full_text:
A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng virtualization hosts.

Xen Orchestra is a web-based management platform developed by French software company Vates, used to manage XCP-ng virtualization environments, including virtual machines, hosts, and pools.

The vulnerability, tracked as VSA-2026-062, affects Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA) and allows remote attackers with network access to the management interface to bypass authentication using a specially crafted cookie. A CVE identifier and CVSS score have not been assigned yet.

According to a Vates security advisory, the flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication tokens sent through REST API requests.

The flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication cookies.

By sending a specially crafted cookie (authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D) containing an empty JSON object ({}), attackers can trick the platform into retrieving an existing authentication token and logging them in as its owner, without requiring actual credentials.

Once authenticated, attackers can retrieve "reusable login token IDs" through the /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens REST API endpoint, which can be used for further access.

"An adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root," warns Vates.

The company has released Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 (stable) and 6.10.0 (latest), including patched xo-server packages 5.211.2 and 5.213.1 to fix these security vulnerabilities.

Administrators should install the update immediately, and if not possible, restrict Xen Orchestra access to dedicated management networks and block known malicious IP addresses.

Security researchers Filip Magic and Christoffer Olsen of TDC NET Security discovered the vulnerability.

Exploited in attacks

Vates confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited and shared the following indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help administrators identify attacks:

Attacker's infrastructure: Connections to 91.211.251.112:8001 or ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid.onion:3333.

Suspicious authentication cookies: HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}.

Virtual machines: A VM named pivot2.

Modified VM configurations: Virtual machines configured with the hvm_serial: file parameter.

Unusual files: /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6.

Administrators can also run the following commands on XCP-ng hosts to check for unusual VM configurations, virtual machines configured to use a file for its serial port, and malicious files:

xe vm-list params=name-label,platform | grep -B1 'hvm_serial: file' zgrep -- '-serial file:' /var/log/xensource.log* ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload /.ustar* /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar*

However, Vates warns that exploitation will not generate any identifiers in logs, such as the use of specially crafted cookies, and instead must be detected through HTTP monitoring.

The company also says these IOCs are only associated with this known attack campaign and may differ for other threat actors.

Companies that believe they are compromised should rotate passwords and secrets used by their virtualization environments.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Sandbox-Evading Python Backdoor
articles.context: The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant.

The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026.

The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems.

"However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said.

Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells -

nsmind.jsp, a signed API with command execution and file transfer capabilities using exec, cd, upload, and download parameters

AhsayCBS.jsp, a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory

Keyed command shell, which compares a hard-coded key against its own copy and, if it matches, runs the command via "cmd.exe"

Keyed shell with file write, which expands on the keyed command web shell with the ability to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and deploy more tools

status_<six_random_letters>.jsp or st_<six_random_letters>.jsp (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), which are used to run commands, recursively delete any path provided as input, and delete themselves using cmd, del, and rm parameters.

"[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later."

The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool.

The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine.

It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com").

In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access.

Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups.

"On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said.

"Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

articles.title: Binance warns of iOS flaw that could leak crypto wallet secrets
articles.context: Public exploit available “worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of...
articles.full_text:
Binance is warning about a vulnerability in Apple’s iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 that could allow third-party apps to read private files stored by other apps, including cryptocurrency seed phrases, secret keys, and login credentials.

The crypto exchange clarifies that the issue is at the iOS level and does not impact only the Binance app.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem,” Binance says.

At this time, no cryptocurrency losses have been confirmed, but Binance urges users to install the update immediately as a precaution.

The company recommends that users delete any unnecessary and untrusted apps and apply the latest versions for iOS and other apps.

Where compromise is suspected, Binance advises users to transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

Public exploit available

“worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of other applications.

Yesterday, a proof-of-concept exploit has been published that uses a tool called WQ Files to perform attacks relying on the technique. Specifically, WQ Files uses “worse_query” to browse, export, edit, and delete other apps’ data without requiring a jailbreak.

An attacker could

The tool must be installed on an iPhone for the attack to work, but an attacker could distribute it through untrusted sources as a sideloaded app, bypassing Apple's App Store.

WQ Files has been confirmed to work on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2, the same versions that Binance warned about.

Apple on November 9 released iOS security updates (iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, and 18.7.12) that address nine flaws. One of the fixed vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-113963, could allow an app to access sensitive user data.

It is unclear if this is the same security issue Binance is warning of, though.

The CVE-2026-113963 problem was reported by László Várady flaw, who found that the access occurred through App Intents, not App Group containers.

BleepingComputer has contacted Apple for clarifications and a request for comment, and we will add an update once we receive more details.

articles.title: iOS Sandbox Escape Is Public, and Apple Hasn’t Confirmed a Fix
articles.context: No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed
articles.full_text:
A public iOS sandbox escape could expose wallet keys, Binance warns. No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed.

On 10 November, Binance warned users about a public iOS sandbox escape that lets one app read the files of other apps. Seed phrases, private keys and login credentials could be exposed to a malicious app, the exchange said.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.” reads the warning.

Binance advises users to remove apps installed from untrusted sources, update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions, and, if a breach is suspected, move funds to a new wallet on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

— Binance (@binance) November 10, 2026

A researcher known as ‘forcequitOS’ published the PoC exploit code, called worse_query, on GitHub. Apple released security updates for both iOS versions the following day, but its release notes mysteriously don’t report a fix for the issue. The good news is that neither Binance nor the researcher has reported any attacks or data theft.

“worse_query is the direct successor to bad_query and essentially replaces it. To use worse_query, you’ll have to set up an App Group container for your app.” forcequitOS wrote.

The proof-of-concept can access the data folders used by all apps and, on iOS 27, some system folders as well. To work, an app must create an App Group container. The researcher says the code is intended for developers and “isn’t useful by itself.” However, other developers have already used it to build apps that can be installed on iPhones.

One example is WQ Files, a file manager developed by Christoph Kolbicz, TheHackerNews reports.

“WQ Files is a file browser, app data manager and cache cleaner for iOS 26 and 27. “WQ” stands for worse_query, the sandbox technique it is built on. It reaches other apps’ and system containers with no jailbreak and no kernel exploit. Tested on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2.” reads the description.

It can access data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak or a kernel exploit. It can also edit, delete and clear that data. Users can install it through sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the required App Group when users sign in with their Apple ID.

I agree (and I wasn't planning on it), but I don't mind the loss of any potential bounty tbh, when Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here.

— forcequit (@forcequitOS) November 8, 2026

The forcequitOS says they have no intention of seeking a bug bounty from Apple and are willing to give up any potential reward because of Apple’s delayed response and the inappropriate behavior of people publicly misusing or exaggerating the exploit.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apple)

articles.title: Researcher bypassed Meta smart glasses’ safeguards to run her own code
articles.context: Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses
articles.full_text:
We’ve written before about what Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses can see and hear, and who might get to use that information. Those worries focus on how the glasses handle information during normal use. A security researcher has now shown how to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on them.

Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. For the technical details I’ll gladly refer you to her own post about it.

The glasses are controlled by the Meta AI app on the owner’s phone. Developers can add their own apps to the glasses through a developer tool, and the phone sends that software to the glasses to install.

The glasses were supposed to check that the software really came from Meta. In older firmware (up to and including version 126), they didn’t check, so the researcher could swap in an app of her own.

Meta introduced a check in firmware version 127 to verify the app’s digital signature to prove that it came from Meta . The researcher found the on/off switch for that signature check came from a settings file passed along by the phone. The glasses only checked the file was correctly formed, not whether it had been tampered with. Changing a single byte in the file turned the signature check off.

Once her app was running, she could send commands to the glasses from the paired phone over a wireless connection.

The glasses have a camera, microphones and a wireless connection, and they sit on your face all day. A wearable that can be made to run unapproved code goes beyond a privacy-policy question. It becomes a security question about who controls the device. As we’ve seen, some cheaper smart glasses already are a security disaster.

In this case the person running the code would be the person that controls the phone. If malicious software running on the glasses could access the camera or stored recordings, it could potentially send footage to an attacker’s server. Pamoutaf’s research doesn’t demonstrate that scenario, but it raises questions about what that software might be able to access.

In her post she promised a follow-up exploring other potential ways to attack the glasses.

How to stay safe

Keep the glasses’ firmware and the Meta AI app updated, and avoid unofficial apps or modifications.

If smart glasses are just another gadget to you, I’d leave them on the shelf. If you rely on them as an accessibility aid, you deserve technology that helps you without putting your privacy or other people’s at risk.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

articles.title: Introducing JFrog Threat Hub: Turning Vulnerability Intelligence into Blast Radius Analysis
articles.context: A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment
articles.full_text:
A new supply chain attack hits the news. A CVE with a dramatic name starts trending. A malicious package turns up in npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face. Within minutes, your Slack channels fill up, your CISO wants an update, and someone asks the question every DevSecOps professional dreads:

“How are we affected?”

Providing a definitive answer should be simple. In practice it often takes hours, and sometimes even days to get the complete picture.

The pain: awareness is easy, blast radius is hard

Security teams are not short on information. Advisories, research blogs, vendor bulletins, social media threads, and mailing lists all announce new threats faster than anyone can read them. The challenging part is leveraging that information to understand how it affects your particular environment.

Until now, that process usually looked something like this:

Separating the signal from the noise. Relevant intelligence is scattered across dozens of sources. Some of it is vetted, some of it is speculation, and some of it is a repost of a repost. Someone has to read it, judge its credibility, and decide whether it deserves attention.

Translating general threats into actionable responses. A blog post describes an attack. It doesn’t hand you a clean list of the affected packages and versions. Someone has to extract the package names, version ranges, and CVE identifiers, and hope nothing was missed.

Figuring out where affected components are hiding. Today, software applications are assembled from many open-source components. Unfortunately, the vulnerability that was just discovered is rarely a direct dependency. It’s usually buried several layers deep in a transitive dependency which is part of a Docker image, or sitting in a build from last quarter. Your artifacts are spread across multiple repositories, projects, teams, and pipelines, making it difficult to identify all the affected components across the entire software supply chain.

Stitching together a holistic view from disparate tools. One tool tracks vulnerabilities, another tracks builds, and a spreadsheet maps services to owners. Correlating these sources manually is a slow and error-prone process, especially in the middle of a high profile security incident where nobody has the time to do it.

Prioritizing remediation with imperfect data. Published severity scores don’t always match real-world exploitability. A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment. Without context analysis, teams either over-react or under-react because they lack the proper information.

All of the above happens while the clock is ticking. The window between disclosure and exploitation keeps shrinking, and every hour spent hunting for an answer is another hour attackers can use to exploit weaknesses in your application. The real cost is often not the vulnerability itself but the time it takes to figure out the most effective strategy for defending against it.

Meet JFrog Threat Hub: taking you from “what happened?” to “what’s affected?” in a single unified interface

JFrog Threat Hub is designed to close the gap. It brings both publicly published security research and JFrog’s own threat intelligence directly into the JFrog Platform, to help determine how it affects your development environment.

What is JFrog Threat Hub?

JFrog Threat Hub is a detailed threat intelligence dashboard accessed from within JFrog Xray. It includes a daily-updated feed of vetted posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages. Most of the security intelligence is based on reports from the JFrog Security Research team, which monitors public registries such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face, runs automated scanners on every new and updated package, and analyzes CVEs for real-world exploitability. Relevant external advisories are also included in the feed.

Each post includes the name of the source, publish date, CVSS score, and descriptive tags, along with a public label that groups the affected packages and versions. A severity mismatch indicator flags cases where JFrog’s research rates a threat differently from its published score, so teams can prioritize by actual, rather than perceived, risk.

One of the most important features is the Check Impact button. With one click, it runs an impact search across your organization and lists every affected artifact, along with its repository, vulnerable component version, scan date, and runtime status. Teams can export these results, set Xray policies, or move straight into triage and remediation all within a single unified platform.

Threat Hub includes updated CVE advisories and impact search across the entire supply chain

Instead of reading about an attack in one place and searching for exposure in another, Threat Hub brings both steps into one seamless workflow. It not only provides early awareness, but also helps map out the true blast radius, taking you directly from reading about a threat to understanding your exact exposure.

Curated intelligence, delivered where you already work

Threat Hub consolidates security posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages, updates it daily, and then sorts it according to customer preference. In addition, intelligence from the JFrog Security Research Team is integrated as well, including:

Continuous monitoring of open-source repositories such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face for the latest security issues

Running automated scanners across new and updated packages

Deeply investigating suspicious findings

Analyzing new and existing CVEs for real-world exploitability

Disclosing newly discovered malware to repository maintainers

For our customers, this means original, vetted research sits alongside the external advisories that matter, without the noise of an open-ended news feed. Each post shows its source, publish date, and tags such as which ecosystems are affected. When a post is tied to a known attack, it applies a label that puts together groups of affected packages and versions, and may link to a fix or advisory.

Just one click to gauge CVE impact

When working from the JFrog Xray interface, the Threat Hub dashboard can be accessed by selecting Xray > Overview. One of the most powerful features of the Threat Hub console is the “Check Impact” button. Click it, and Threat Hub opens an Impact Search specifically for your organization. If you are affected, it shows the matching artifacts and their scan dates, so you can see where the problem lives across your scanned artifacts and decide what to fix first.

For supported CVE and malicious package posts, there’s no manual extraction of package names, no custom queries, and no stitching together results from separate tools. The research and the results are presented side by side.

CVE Severity you can act on

Published scores don’t always tell the whole story, so some posts also show a Severity Mismatch Indicator when JFrog Security Research’s assessment differs from the severity of a publicly available CVE or advisory. JFrog’s research severity reflects real-world exploitability and impact, not just the published score, which gives you the context you need when prioritizing your remediation strategy.

What this changes for your team

Operations and Security teams gain these important advantages:

Faster incident scoping. The question “How are we affected?” can get an answer faster, with less cross-tool detective work.

Less context switching. Reading the research, understanding the impact, and identifying affected artifacts all happen in one centralized interface.

Improved prioritization. Vetted research and severity context from JFrog’s own researchers helps focus on the threats that are more likely to be exploitable.

More precise communications. When leadership asks for a status update, you can present them with the specific affected artifacts and scan dates instead of “we’re still looking.”

See JFrog Threat Hub in action

The next major supply chain attack is a question of when, not if. When it arrives, the teams that respond best won’t be the ones who read the most blog posts. They’ll be the ones who can understand how a specific threat affects their particular environment in the fastest way possible.

Learn more about JFrog Security and see how you can shorten the path from “What happened?” to “How are we affected” by scheduling a demo with one of our domain experts.

articles.title: Critical vulnerabilities in N-able N-central prompt hosted shutdown
articles.context: Overview On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and...
articles.full_text:
Overview

On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details.

As of November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor has advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it develops and validates a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments remain offline, according to the same notice. N-able's notice does not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026. Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations operating on-premises N-central servers take them offline immediately and keep them offline until the hotfix is available, and the server has been successfully upgraded. Hosted customers should follow the vendor's service restoration updates. N-able is developing and validating a hotfix, with a target of midday November 10 EST.

Affected versions: The researcher reports testing N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. N-able's current notice does not specify the full affected-version range.

Fixed versions: N-able's incident notice does not yet identify a remediation build. Follow the incident notice for release confirmation and installation instructions.

Rapid7 also recommends reviewing N-central servers and downstream managed systems for signs of compromise and engaging incident responders if suspicious activity is identified.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to N-able's security incident notice.

Updates

November 10, 2026: Initial publication.

articles.title: Cloud Vulnerabilities Surge Fourfold in Less Than a Year
articles.context: ” Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds
articles.full_text:
The median number of high or critical vulnerabilities in cloud workloads increased fourfold between May and November this year, due to the impact of frontier AI, Datadog has claimed.

The cloud observability and security specialist revealed the findings in its State of Cloud Security 2026 published on November 10. It’s based on analysis of the cloud security posture of thousands of customer organizations around the world.

Datadog claimed that the median number of high/critical severity flaws in cloud workloads surged from four in May, when Anthropic’s Mythos model was released, to 14 in June and 16 in November.

The data was sourced from analysis of vulnerabilities in third-party libraries used by applications monitored through Datadog Code Security’s Software Composition Analysis (SCA) feature, the report noted.

“This data reveals that the increased number of vulnerabilities in the CVE database isn't a theoretical risk,” it added. “It affects an increasing number of real-world applications running in cloud environments, reinforcing the need for cloud security foundations that limit the blast radius of compromised applications.”

Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds.

The report also highlighted the challenge of long-lived credentials; specifically related to cloud-hosted AI inference services and CI/CD pipelines.

Datadog warned that such credentials are consistently ranked as one of the most common causes of cloud breaches, with automated tools continuously scanning the web for weaknesses.

“Red-team frameworks like Pacu and Datadog’s own Pathrunner along with secret scanners like TruffleHog reliably find over-permissioned credentials and exposed keys at scale,” it said. “That same tooling is available to autonomous attackers, who enumerate for long-lived credentials first because they’re the highest-value, longest-lived prize in the environment.”

The report revealed that nearly half of organizations using Gemini use long-lived Gemini API keys, while the percentage of cloud users with access keys older than three years has reached nearly 30% for AWS IAM and Google Cloud Service Account users.

“Rather than static Bedrock or Gemini API keys, you should access AI inference services through the calling workload’s short-lived identity when supported (IAM role, managed identity, or service account) so the model is reached with the same federated credentials as other cloud resources and not a separate long-lived key,” Datadog explained.

Cloud Dependencies Expose Users to Machine-Speed Attacks

Supply-chain attacks are increasingly run autonomously and at machine speed, with hijacked dependencies one of the most popular routes to compromise, Datadog claimed.

Part of the challenge is the speed with which new dependency versions are adopted by users. If adopted automatically without proper vetting, they can result in the rapid compromise of cloud credentials and services.

Some 60% of organizations Datadog analyzed run versions that were released less than 24 hours earlier, with these versions appearing in more than a fifth (21%) of cloud applications.

The risk is amplified the more dependencies there are, and Datadog found that app workloads running in the cloud have on average 149 software dependencies. The figure across the average organization is 568.

“Organizations should implement dependency cooldowns to lower the risk of malicious dependencies reaching their cloud environments, because the community usually identifies and contains hijacked libraries within a few hours,” the report recommended.

articles.title: Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8
articles.context: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar
articles.full_text: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited. The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight. That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess. Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

articles.title: Update Chrome now to fix a flaw attackers are exploiting
articles.context: A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available
articles.full_text:
On November 9, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. It includes nine security fixes, including one for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.

A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available.

Hong Kong’s Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) rates the overall risk as “Extremely High.” Its bulletin says some of the vulnerabilities address in the update could allow denial of service, security restriction bypass, and remote code execution.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.51 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android on November 9. Google says it includes the same security fixes as the desktop release unless otherwise noted. Android users should check Google Play for the update.

Technical details

Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability.

Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component.

XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

Google only says that it is “aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” It has not named the attackers, the targets, the delivery method, or what the exploit can do.

articles.title: Microsoft’s AI bug hunter finds Rust flaw that went undetected for nearly 11 years
articles.context: Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory.

The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling.

“The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years,” the researchers wrote in a blog post. Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely.

The research used Hyenas, FORGE Lab’s AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system, to investigate unsafe code in Rust’s standard library. Hyenas is the lab’s research version of codename MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic vulnerability-discovery system.

Microsoft said some of the bugs were found with help from Hyenas. Researchers then examined the underlying code, reproduced the issues, assessed their security impact, and reported them to Rust maintainers.

Microsoft said the practical risk is limited. Each flaw requires unusual conditions to trigger, and a bug in the standard library becomes “a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way,” the researchers wrote.

Unsafe code challenges Rust’s safety guarantees

Rust’s ownership model and type system are designed to prevent memory-safety problems commonly associated with languages such as C and C++. However, its standard library relies on unsafe code internally for operations that the compiler cannot verify.

Components such as Vec and String use these operations but expose them through safe APIs. Microsoft said these APIs must meet a strict soundness requirement: “no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.”

Microsoft grouped the findings into three categories: unsafe code that assumes operations will not panic, code that trusts user-provided implementations to behave correctly, and code that makes incorrect assumptions about the underlying system.

The first involved a panic-safety problem in Rust’s MapWindows::clone implementation. The function created a buffer before fully initializing its contents and then called a user-provided clone operation to populate it. If that operation triggered a panic, Rust’s unwinding mechanism could invoke the buffer’s destructor, which would attempt to access uninitialized memory. Microsoft said the reported fix prevents the partially initialized buffer from being destroyed before initialization is complete.

Another finding involved str::replace. The researchers found that the function could make an incorrect assumption about a custom implementation of the nightly Pattern trait. A custom implementation could supply a non-ASCII byte where the code expected an ASCII character, causing the replacement operation to produce invalid UTF-8 data. Subsequent string operations could then trigger undefined behavior, Microsoft said.

System-level bugs affect stable Rust

Microsoft said the first two categories of weaknesses were already being studied in 2021 through Rudra, a static analyzer developed by members of the research team. The standard library had also addressed panic-safety problems as far back as 2015, but similar weaknesses continue to appear in its implementations.

The third category involves interactions between Rust and underlying operating systems and C libraries. Besides the process::exit issue, researchers identified a problem in Rust’s CommandExt::exec functionality involving the process-wide environment variable array.

Microsoft found that the function could modify this shared state while holding a read lock, potentially allowing other threads to access inconsistent data. Under certain conditions, concurrent operations could leave the environment pointer referencing freed memory.

Microsoft said both the process::exit and CommandExt::exec findings affect stable Rust. A proposed fix for the environment-variable issue, which avoids modifying the shared array by calling execve directly, was under review when the blog was published.

Two issues reported by Microsoft’s team remained open at publication. The blog also discussed related reports from other researchers and fixes still under review.

Findings feed into Microsoft’s security products

Microsoft said the research findings can also feed into Microsoft Perception, its multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work across broader security workflows. It would therefore help the company improve the development of MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender.

For example, Microsoft’s Web App Pen Test Agent can use MDASH findings to prioritize testing, assess exploitability against live applications, and provide information to support remediation, the researchers wrote.

“Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs,” the researchers wrote, but to identify meaningful issues and improve the safety of foundational software developers and organizations depend on. The Rust project had not responded to a request for comment from CSO at the time of writing.

articles.title: Binance Warns of iOS Sandbox Escape That Could Expose Crypto Wallet Keys, No Fix Confirmed
articles.context: Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix
articles.full_text:
An iOS sandbox escape published on GitHub lets an app read other apps' files on iPhones running iOS 26 and 27. That puts seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk of exposure to malicious apps, Binance warned today. Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix.

A researcher who goes by forcequit released the escape, called worse_query, on Sunday, a day before those updates came out. Neither the exchange nor the researcher reported any attacks or thefts involving it.

The exchange told users to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps. No fix for the escape has been confirmed.

For anyone who suspects a breach, the exchange's security warning advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and resetting all active login sessions.

The researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone, and some system folders on iOS 27. To use it, an app has to set up an App Group container.

He says the code is for developers and "isn't useful by itself." Other developers have built apps on it that people can install.

One of them is WQ Files, a file manager that developer Christoph Kolbicz built on worse_query. It reaches other apps' data without a jailbreak or a kernel exploit, and it can edit, delete and clear that data.

WQ Files installs via sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the App Group it needs when used with an Apple ID. No one involved has said whether an app from the App Store could use worse_query.

The three versions in the exchange's warning are the ones listed as tested in the WQ Files release notes. The researcher gives a wider range.

Of these sources, only Erosion's developers list iOS 27.2.1, which came out yesterday, and none lists iOS 26.7.3. They added 27.2.1 this week in a README change with the note "pretty sure 27.2.1 is supported".

Yesterday's updates, iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3, fixed two iMessage flaws and several Bluetooth bugs. The security notes for iOS 27.2.1 do not mention worse_query or any sandbox issues, nor do the iOS 26.7.3 notes. Apple does not disclose, discuss, or confirm security issues until it has investigated and a patch or release is available, the notes say.

In a reply on X, the researcher wrote that he had not planned to release worse_query early. He added that "Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here."

The exchange did not name any wallet app as exposed, and neither did the researcher nor the developers of the apps built on worse_query.

articles.title: SAP patches ICM2SHELL and PROXYGATE maximum severity flaws
articles.context: For instance, it patched CVE-2026-58231 in the Commerce Cloud cloud-based e-commerce platform in August, which threat intelligence firm Defused flagged as actively exploited in...
articles.full_text:
SAP patched 35 vulnerabilities in its November 2026 security updates, including four maximum-severity issues affecting its NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, and Gateway software.

The company addressed memory corruption (CVE-2026-76964) and missing authentication (CVE-2026-120017) flaws in the NetWeaver Application Server ABAP's Internet Communication Manager and SAML2 Service Provider components.

NetWeaver is the core app platform that underpins SAP's business software and handles application integration, authentication, user management, and data processing.

The other two maximum severity vulnerabilities stem from a broken access control weakness (CVE-2026-89103) in SAP Gateway and a memory corruption issue (CVE-2026-89126) in SAP Web Dispatcher.

Gateway is a core framework that enables external apps to securely connect to SAP backend systems, while Web Dispatcher (deployed in almost every enterprise SAP environment) is a specialized component that acts as a load balancer and reverse proxy for web requests entering an SAP system architecture.

Cybersecurity firm Onapsis, which found and reported three of these security issues, collectively tracks CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126 as ICM2SHELL and the CVE-2026-89103 pre-auth remote code execution vulnerability as PROXYGATE.

"ICM2SHELL turns a routine part of web traffic into a point of ingress for attackers. [..] The result is remote code execution against the component that faces the network by design: no SAP user, no password and no user interaction," Onapsis said.

"PROXYGATE works by convincing the SAP Gateway that an unauthenticated, external attacker is one of the internal application servers. [..] There is no SAP user, no password, and no user interaction, yet full control of the SAP system as the account that owns the installation is achieved. On a production ERP system, that means direct exposure of the business data, transaction integrity, and the availability of critical business applications."

SAP rated these four vulnerabilities 10/10 on the CVSS severity scale, stating that unauthenticated attackers can exploit them to fully compromise the targeted systems remotely.

More recently patched max severity SAP security issues

These are the latest in a string of other maximum-severity flaws SAP has fixed in multiple components in recent months.

For instance, it patched CVE-2026-58231 in the Commerce Cloud cloud-based e-commerce platform in August, which threat intelligence firm Defused flagged as actively exploited in attacks days after the patch.

It also addressed two more max severity flaws in September and October: a memory corruption flaw in the SAP Kernel code (tracked as CVE-2026-44756 and dubbed OVERPASS by Onapsis security researchers who reported it) and an OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability affecting multi-tenant BTP applications (CVE-2026-89111).

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 14 SAP security flaws as actively exploited since November 2021, three of which ransomware groups also abused in the wild.

SAP is a German multinational software company that reported revenues exceeding €36 billion in fiscal year 2025 and serves 99 of the 100 largest companies worldwide.

articles.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability

CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Apple Patches iMessage Group Chat Privacy Flaws and Bluetooth Pairing Vulnerabilities
articles.context: An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it
articles.full_text:
An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.

The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected.

The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27.

The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960.

Which Updates Carry the Fixes

Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update.

The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes.

The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away.

The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component.

All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do.

Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

articles.title: Hackers now exploit critical Barracuda ESG flaws to gain root access
articles.context: The first stems from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that can be exploited to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second lets...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity company Barracuda Networks warned that attackers have begun exploiting two recently patched Email Security Gateway (ESG) vulnerabilities that let them run commands with root privileges.

Barracuda released security updates to address the two flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560) one week ago.

The first stems from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that can be exploited to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second lets unauthenticated attackers inject OS commands that execute with root privileges.

Barracuda also said that successful attacks require access to the administrative user interface (Admin UI) of targeted devices and advised customers to restrict access to trusted internal networks and use appropriate network access controls to limit exposure.

"Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device," the company explained.

On Monday evening, Barracuda updated the initial advisory to warn admins that the two flaws are being exploited in attacks targeting a limited number of customers.

"Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations," it warned.

"If a patch has not been automatically applied, customers should manually apply the appropriate patch as soon as possible. If customers have turned off automatic patching, Barracuda recommends setting devices to automatically receive patches."

Three years ago, Barracuda patched another Email Security Gateway flaw (CVE-2023-7102) that the UNC4841 hacking group exploited in zero-day attacks to execute arbitrary code. The same year, UNC4841 abused another zero-day (CVE-2023-2868) to target Barracuda ESG appliances as part of a series of cyber-espionage attacks.

The company later revealed that the flaw had been exploited as a zero-day for at least seven months, since at least October 2022, to drop previously unknown SeaSpy and Saltwater malware and steal data from compromised devices.

According to cybersecurity firm Mandiant, almost a third of systems breached in the 2023 campaign belonged to government agencies, most of them hacked between October and December 2022.

Barracuda was founded in 2003 and now has more than 200,000 customers worldwide, including small- to medium-sized businesses (SMBs), large enterprises, and managed service providers (MSPs).
