articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure
articles.context: Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17
articles.full_text:
Someone tried to exploit two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language four days before the vulnerabilities were published and the flaws are now being exploited in the wild at scale, according to Amazon.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover on any websites relying on any PHP version released in the last decade – going back to version 5.4.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data. These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

The bugs were discovered by security researchers at California-based security firm Calif and Google Cloud’s Wiz, with collaboration from OpenAI’s Patch the Planet project, in August. Public disclosure was scheduled for October 21, when the PHP Foundation planned to release the security patches.

However, on October 20, a pseudonymous user of the Hacker News forum leaked some information about the flaws before the patches were ready.

This led to many organizations across the world, including French public administrations, the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre and the University of Vienna taking their websites offline to prepare for and then apply the patches.

Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17. The attempt occurred in MadPot, an internal honeypot system created by Amazon Web Services (AWS) to monitor, study and disrupt global cybercrime.

Early Exploitation Attempt Likely From A “Threat Actor”

The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. According to the Amazon researchers, this suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

In addition, they said they identified multiple proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for PHP2Shell on October 21, around 12 hours before the vulnerability’s scheduled disclosure at 2pm GMT.

The earliest exploit was detected at approximately 2am GMT, with further attempts targeting the company’s MadPot sensors between 2am and 8am GMT from additional infrastructure.

According to the researchers, variations in the payloads and anonymization infrastructure suggested that multiple threat actors were involved. However, it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Further PoC exploits emerged within hours of the release of the PHP2Shell patches, which were used against Amazon’s sensors almost immediately.

The researchers warned that PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Emerging Evidence of PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts

Other security and threat intelligence teams have started to report active exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the wild.

Matthew Prince, co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said on X his company saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the vulnerabilities within the 10 hours that preceded the disclosure.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he added.

Other security firms, including Beelzebub, Ellio, Recorded Future, VulnCheck, WatchTowr and Wiz have also observed evidence of exploitation attempts in the wild for both vulnerabilities.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: Two Critical PHP Flaws Allow Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.context: These steps do not fully address either vulnerability, so they should be used only until the upgrade is complete, and each one should be tested first
articles.full_text:
Exploitation status

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said it had not observed exploitation as of publication, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said a proof of concept was public with no active exploitation identified. The European Union's CERT-EU said technical details and proofs of concept were circulating, which raised the likelihood of exploitation, but did not confirm attacks. The BSI reported no confirmed exploitation but unconfirmed reports of existing exploits, and expected broad exploitation within hours of the patches because public details make exploit development fast. Each agency urged immediate patching.

Several security vendors have reported potential exploitation. Their honeypot and customer telemetry reportedly showed exploitation attempts, including at least one report of activity on October 17, before the public disclosure, and others reporting attacks at scale on October 21, with attackers adapting payloads to evade web application firewall (WAF) rules. Given the public details and proof-of-concept code, any internet-facing PHP server that remained unpatched after October 20 should be treated as potentially exposed.

Who is affected?

Any PHP installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The PHP project assessed Apache with mod_php as the highest risk. Third-party products, appliances, containers and hosting platforms that embed PHP may also be affected. The Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) is maintaining a repository of affected third-party products.

Broadcom has said that no Broadcom Enterprise Security Group products have been confirmed affected.

Patching

Patching is the recommended remediation. The PHP project's fixed versions are:

PHP 8.5: upgrade to 8.5.12

PHP 8.4: upgrade to 8.4.27

PHP 8.3: upgrade to 8.3.36

PHP 8.2: upgrade to 8.2.35

Organizations should also take the following steps.

Restart after upgrading. Restart PHP-FPM pools and Apache so that no worker keeps running the old binary. PHP-FPM must be patched too.

Find every instance. Inventory internet-facing hosts first, then internal ones. Check the version the web server actually runs, for example, with php-fpm -v, or by checking the Apache module, and not only with the command-line php -v, since the two can differ.

Rebuild containers and check appliances. Rebuild images on patched base images, and check third-party appliances and hosting providers that embed PHP.

Handle unsupported branches. The PHP project published no upstream fix for PHP 8.1, 7.x and 5.x, although it has provided limited source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Check with your operating system vendor for backported packages. For example, Red Hat has published an advisory for PHP 7.4 (RHSA-2026:87080) and Fedora has issued updates. Where no backport exists, apply the interim mitigations below and plan an upgrade to a supported branch.

CISA recommended taking unpatched systems offline, and the BSI recommended considering disconnecting vulnerable servers from the internet, if patching cannot be done promptly. The CERT-EU advisory recommended isolating internet-facing applications until the fix is applied and verified.

Interim mitigations

If immediate patching is not possible, the PHP project's advisories list configuration changes that reduce exposure. These steps do not fully address either vulnerability, so they should be used only until the upgrade is complete, and each one should be tested first. The PHP advisories include further settings, such as limits on request size and structure for CVE-2026-109618.

Disable session upload-progress tracking by setting session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in the active php.ini.

Disable OPcache by setting opcache.enable = 0. This removes the OPcache stale-cache technique, which gives arbitrary file reads. A noticeable performance cost is to be expected.

Check fatal-error backtraces. One technique requires them to be enabled, so turn them off if they are on and follow the PHP advisory for the exact setting.

Reload PHP. Restart PHP-FPM or Apache so the new settings take effect.

Put a WAF in front of the application. Several WAF vendors released virtual-patch rules covering the anomalous multipart and session traffic these exploits use. Confirm with your vendor that the rule is deployed and in blocking mode.

Reduce exposure. Restrict access to PHP applications that do not need to be public, and run PHP workers with least privilege so that a compromise exposes as few files, credentials and connected services as possible.

The BSI also recommended enabling SELinux or AppArmor where possible on Linux to limit the impact of any RCE vulnerability.

Protection

Symantec, Carbon Black and CBX protect against this threat. The Protection Bulletin lists every protection by name and is updated as new information becomes available, so it should be treated as the definitive reference. Additional product protections are in development.

Behavior-based protection

Symantec Endpoint behavioral protection (SONAR) includes 16 signatures covering suspicious behavior, suspicious process launches, registry and file writes, process starts and User Account Control (UAC) bypass attempts associated with PHP2Shell exploitation.

Carbon Black App Control

Carbon Black App Control customers can use four execution control rules to monitor, and later block, behavior potentially related to PHP2Shell exploitation. Every rule should start in Report mode. The rules should be updated with known indicators of compromise (IOCs) as they are published, and reported activity verified before any rule is switched to Block.

Linux PHP suspicious application execution: php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd or apache2 launching sh, bash, python, perl, curl, wget or nc.

Linux suspicious command lines: any process whose command line matches /dev/tcp/, fsockopen or mkfifo.

Windows PHP suspicious application execution: php-cgi.exe or php.exe launching cmd.exe, powershell.exe, certutil.exe or cscript.exe.

Windows suspicious command lines: nc.exe run with -e, or PowerShell command lines containing System.Net.Sockets.TcpClient or New-Object Net.WebClient.

Endpoint detection and response hunting

Hunting queries and watchlist queries are available for both Carbon Black Cloud and Carbon Black OnPrem. They look for the same behavior as the App Control rules: PHP and web server processes spawning shells, scripting interpreters or download tools on Linux, PHP processes spawning command interpreters on Windows, and the suspicious command lines listed above. Customers should hunt for this behavior on any PHP server that was unpatched after October 20.

File-based protection

Symantec file-based protection detects related tooling as Hacktool.Php2shell.

The full list of SONAR signature names, the complete App Control rule definitions and the exact Carbon Black query syntax are in the Protection Bulletin.

articles.title: ZDI-26-790: OpenSSL CMS AuthEnvelopedData Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to tamper with CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages on affected installations of OpenSSL. An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of AES-GCM message authentication codes. The issue results from an improper integrity check. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to tamper with authenticated data.

Additional Details

OpenSSL has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt

Disclosure Timeline

2026-04-09 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-22 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: ZDI-26-789: OpenSSL CMP Use of Externally-Controlled Format String Information Disclosure Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of OpenSSL
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of OpenSSL. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of Distinguished Names within CMP messages. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it as a format specifier. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to disclose information in the context of the client or server.

Additional Details

OpenSSL has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://openssl-library.org/news/vulnerabilities/#CVE-2026-63073

Disclosure Timeline

2026-04-08 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-22 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: ZDI-26-788: Cisco Snort OLE VBA Decompression Stack-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Cisco Snort
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Cisco Snort. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the decompression of VBA data in OLE file streams. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.

Additional Details

Cisco has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-snort3-vba-bufdos-jAuFdvn9

Disclosure Timeline

2026-06-30 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-22 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: ZDI-26-787: NVIDIA Megatron Bridge YAML File Parsing Code Injection Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of NVIDIA Megatron Bridge
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of NVIDIA Megatron Bridge. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of model configuration files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to execute Python code. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

Additional Details

NVIDIA has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://nvidia.custhelp.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/5841/~/security-bulletin%3A-nvidia-megatron-bridge---june-2026

Disclosure Timeline

2026-04-22 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-22 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: ZDI-26-786: NoMachine nxwebrunner Heap-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of NoMachine
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of NoMachine. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the web service, which listens on TCP port 4443 by default. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.

Additional Details

Fixed in v10.1.7; 9.9.6; 8.27.1https://kb.nomachine.com/TR07X11893

Disclosure Timeline

2026-07-24 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-22 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: Turn Your Vulnerability Backlog Into Pull Requests With Agentic Remediation
articles.context: For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization
articles.full_text:
The Evo Remediation Agent is now in Open Preview, bringing automated dependency resolution to Evo Agentic AppSec. AppSec teams can now run ongoing remediation campaigns across repositories and deliver proposed fixes to developers through validated pull requests.

Fixing a dependency vulnerability can mean choosing an upgrade, resolving dependency conflicts, adapting the application, and/or checking the result. That work competes with everything developers are already building. As teams introduce code and new vulnerabilities at increasingly exponential rates, AppSec needs a way to accelerate remediation across the applications they protect.

With the help of agentic remediation, AppSec teams can start by leveraging campaigns targeting a defined set of repositories and vulnerabilities. Snyk supplies the model and hosted sandbox environment, and developers receive proposed changes through their existing source code management (SCM) workflow. The developers continue to retain control over final review and merging.

Give AppSec a way to drive fixes

A remediation campaign defines which vulnerabilities the agent works on, in which repositories, and on what schedule. AppSec teams set the scope, and Evo Remediation Agent works through eligible vulnerabilities and opens pull requests for developers to review.

For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization. Recurring campaigns repeat that work on a schedule as repositories and vulnerability findings change.

That gives AppSec teams a way to initiate remediation without asking each developer to install and run an agent. Teams can follow repository outcomes across a campaign, review where the agent produced fixes, and investigate where remediation efforts still need attention.

Snyk first brought automated dependency updates into developer workflows with automatic Fix PRs across SCA and Container. Agent Fix extended remediation to source-code vulnerabilities detected by Snyk Code, our first AI-native solution generating and checking proposed fixes. The initial Evo Remediation Agent then brought a broader workflow into the CLI and ADE: plan the fix, apply changes, and validate the result in the developer’s environment. Now, fully validated, the next iteration of the Evo Remediation Agent brings campaigns that automate agentic remediation to AppSec teams.

Starting once again with Open Source vulnerabilities, teams can put the agent to work across repositories and make remediation an ongoing part of their security program.

Security context guides the work

A dependency update can require changes throughout an application. The agent uses Snyk findings to plan updates, applies changes in a hosted sandbox, and checks its work with builds, available tests, and rescans. This feedback helps the agent work through the changes an upgrade requires.

When the agent produces a fix, it opens a pull request and records each action attached to the change. Teams can restrict campaigns to fixes assessed as non-breaking, and the agent does not merge changes. Developers review the proposed changes and decide whether to merge them.

Evidence behind the remediation engine

Generating a fix only helps reduce risk if a developer can merge it. A pull request that breaks the build, fails existing tests, or leaves the vulnerability in place adds review work and doesn’t shrink the backlog. A high mergeable fix rate is what turns agent fix suggestions into backlog reduction because more of the fix pull requests actually get merged with less developer rework.

The VulnBump benchmark tests the mergeable fix rate of the engine that powers Evo Remediation Agent. Across 307 dependency-upgrade tasks, the CLI-based Remediation Agent passed all four verification checks on 90.2% of tasks. Claude Code with Snyk findings passed 77.5%, and Claude Code alone passed 59.6%. All three used the same model.

Those checks cover the outcomes that matter to a dependency fix: dependencies resolve, the targeted vulnerabilities disappear on rescan, the application builds, and previously passing tests still pass. The results show the value of combining security context with a purpose-built remediation workflow.

Fix first. Prioritize the rest.

Remediation programs usually start by deciding what to fix. Evo Remediation Agent reverses that order, giving AppSec teams another way to act on the backlog. Recurring campaigns work through eligible vulnerabilities in scope, so what reaches your team is then the work that needs human judgment.

Repository outcomes and journals help teams understand where the agent made progress and where further work remains. AppSec teams get a running view not only of the backlog, but also the pull requests opened, while developers get a record of why each change was made. Remediation consequently becomes an ongoing part of the security program, with your team setting the standard for what ships.

Bring remediation to your team

The Evo Remediation Agent is in Open Preview for Snyk Open Source vulnerabilities in Evo Agentic AppSec. To run campaigns, you need:

Workspaces

SCM integration

Preview access for your Tenant.

During Open Preview, a daily fix allowance applies, and hosted sandboxes use public package registries. Ready to put Evo Remediation Agent to work on your backlog? Talk to your Snyk account team about Open Preview access.

BOOK A LIVE DEMO

Secure AI adoption at scale

Evo helps organizations safely adopt and scale AI by providing visibility, governance, and security across AI-driven development and AI applications.

articles.title: Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
articles.context: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority
articles.full_text:
October 29, 2026: We added guidance for end-of-life PHP versions (8.1 and earlier), including the source backports that the PHP security team published for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1.

October 23, 2026 (update 2): The PHP project disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate remote code execution issue that the October 21 releases don’t fix. It affects only applications with an uncommon configuration that keeps session upload progress enabled. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.4 and later, already blocks POST requests that carry a PHP session ID and the session upload progress field (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS). This helps mitigate CVE-2026-115560 until PHP releases a fix, and no rule group update is needed. PHP recommends setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until its next regular bugfix release. If you applied this setting for CVE-2026-109619, keep it in place.

October 23, 2026: We updated this post for version 2.4 of the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group, which adds the PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended rule for CVE-2026-109618, and AWS made it the default version. AWS is continuously updating the AWS WAF PHP managed rule group to add protection for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. If you use the default version, you will be automatically protected without any action on your part. If you have pinned a specific version, update to the latest version to receive this protection. For the latest version and details on the rules added, see the AWS Managed Rules changelog and subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic (both linked below). Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority.

October 22, 2026: We updated this post to add the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group. Version 2.3 of the rule group adds the PHP2Shell_BODY rule for CVE-2026-109619.

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released emergency fixes for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP core runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively named PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, and both allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. If you run PHP 8.1 or earlier, the PHP project won’t release a new version for your branch, but backported fixes are available for some versions. See Fix end-of-life PHP versions later in this post.

Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. But patching a fleet takes time: you need to inventory where PHP runs, schedule maintenance windows and test applications against the new builds. This post shows you how to use AWS Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF) to help reduce your exposure during that window. The AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group includes rules for both vulnerabilities: PHP2Shell_BODY for CVE-2026-109619 and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended for CVE-2026-109618. AWS continues to release new versions of this rule group as detection improves. Track them in the AWS Managed Rules changelog, or subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic to get notified. If your protection pack (web ACL) uses this rule group at the default version, these rules are already active. This post shows you how to confirm that and how to add the rule group if you don’t use it yet. It also covers the custom rules that still add defense in depth. It also explains where AWS WAF protection ends, so you don’t develop a false sense of safety. For how Amazon threat intelligence detected PHP2Shell exploitation before public disclosure, see Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot. For AWS service status and patching guidance, see AWS Security Bulletin 2026-143-AWS.

IMPORTANT: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority.

The vulnerabilities in brief

Both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are unauthenticated RCE issues rooted in how PHP handles multipart/form-data request processing (the request format browsers use for file uploads) before your application code runs, which is why the AWS WAF rules in this post focus on multipart traffic, request body size, and the session upload progress field. At a high level, CVE-2026-109618 corrupts memory when PHP runs out of memory mid-request, and CVE-2026-109619 lets one request leave behind stale data that a later request on the same worker process reuses. For the root-cause analysis, affected versions, and PHP’s own guidance, see the official PHP advisories and release announcement:

CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) – PHP advisory GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w

CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state) – PHP advisory GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp

PHP security release announcement, October 21, 2026

Where AWS WAF fits in your response

AWS WAF is a defense-in-depth control in this situation, not a replacement for the PHP upgrade. The PHP advisories are explicit: updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. One of the two vulnerabilities is largely outside the reach of any web application firewall, as explained later. Treat the managed rules and the custom rules in this post as mitigating controls that help reduce exposure while you patch, then remove them or keep them as supporting controls after you’ve patched.

AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests at the edge. It doesn’t parse the internal structure of a multipart body, and it has no visibility into PHP worker memory or server-side configuration. The following table maps each attack element to whether AWS WAF can help mitigate it.

Attack element

AWS WAF coverage

Request patterns that match CVE-2026-109618

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.4 or later.

Request patterns that match CVE-2026-109619

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.3 or later.

Session upload progress field in a multipart POST (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, the form field that turns on PHP’s upload-tracking feature)

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule (version 2.4 or later) and the custom rule in this post block POST requests that carry a PHP session ID and that field. This also helps mitigate CVE-2026-115560.

Multipart upload path (multipart/form-data, the request type used for file uploads and the entry point for both vulnerabilities)

Yes, if the application has no legitimate multipart uploads. Block multipart/form-data.

Out-of-memory condition from an oversized body

Partial. PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspects the request body up to the body inspection limit. Cap the request body size with the Core rule set SizeRestrictions_BODY rule or a custom rule. Neither catches header amplification (many small part headers that cost far more memory to represent than their size on the wire) that stays under the cap.

Repeated attempts against the same worker (the reused PHP process that handles many requests)

Partial. A rate-based rule reduces the volume an exploit needs, but it doesn’t stop a single successful request.

fatal_error_backtraces producer (a PHP 8.5 setting that stores crash-trace state across a request)

No. This is a server configuration setting (fatal_error_backtraces=0).

Invalid or deprecated INI diagnostics as a consumer (warnings PHP raises when applying bad configuration settings)

No. This path runs server-side, not over client HTTP.

Where an application does not accept multipart uploads, an edge rule that blocks multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application, plus the session-upload-progress trigger, which is a defense-in-depth control during the patch window.

If your application does use multipart uploads, AWS WAF reduces risk but does not close the vulnerability, because header amplification (a few kilobytes of part headers that expand into far more memory inside PHP) stays within size limits and the firewall cannot parse the headers inside individual body parts. In that case, prioritize the PHP upgrade and apply the server-side mitigations described later.

Start with the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group

The PHP application managed rule group (AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet) contains rules that block request patterns associated with the exploitation of vulnerabilities specific to PHP. PHP2Shell_BODY inspects the request body for requests that match CVE-2026-109619 and is in version 2.3 and later. PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspects the request body for requests that match CVE-2026-109618 and is in version 2.4 and later. The default action of both rules is Block. The AWS WAF documentation notes that this rule group contains a virtual patch for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and that you can add it to your protection pack (web ACL) to help protect your application against exploitation attempts until your application is patched. The rule group uses 100 web ACL capacity units (WCUs). Like the other AWS managed baseline and use-case rule groups, it has no charge beyond standard AWS WAF pricing. For the latest version and details on the rules added, see the AWS Managed Rules changelog and subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic.

What you need to do depends on how your web ACL uses the rule group:

You use the default version. Both PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are already active. Confirm that you haven’t overridden the whole rule group to Count, and review your AWS WAF logs for matches.

You pin a static version. Version_2.3 has PHP2Shell_BODY but not PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended, and Version_2.2 and earlier have neither. Change the version to Version_2.4 or later. We recommend that you use the default version.

You don’t use the rule group yet. Add it to the web ACL in front of each PHP workload, as shown in the following example.

To add the rule group in the AWS WAF console, open your protection pack (web ACL), choose Manage rules, and then do the following, as shown in Figure 1:

Choose Add rule.

Select AWS-managed rule group.

Choose Next.

Under Free, choose PHP application.

For Version, keep Default (recommended). If you need to pin a version, choose Version_2.4 or later.

Under Rule overrides, confirm that PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are listed. To review matches before they block, set both to Count.

Choose Add rule.

Figure 1: Adding the PHP application managed rule group in the AWS WAF console.

If you prefer to work programmatically, run the following commands to see the current default version and the version that a web ACL uses. Both commands are read-only.

aws wafv2 list-available-managed-rule-group-versions \ --vendor-name AWS --name AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet --scope REGIONAL aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name <web-acl-name> --id <web-acl-id> --scope REGIONAL \ --query "WebACL.Rules[?Statement.ManagedRuleGroupStatement.Name=='AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet']"

For web ACLs associated with Amazon CloudFront, use --scope CLOUDFRONT and the US East (N. Virginia) Region. A rule without a Version field uses the default version.

The following rule adds the rule group at the default version. The RuleActionOverrides entry sets PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended to Count so you can review their matches before they block. Remove the override when you’re satisfied. Given how quickly exploitation followed disclosure, measure that review period in hours, not days. If you need to pin the rule group, add a Version field set to Version_2.4 or later to the ManagedRuleGroupStatement. We recommend the default version.

{ "Name": "AWS-AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet", "Priority": 0, "Statement": { "ManagedRuleGroupStatement": { "VendorName": "AWS", "Name": "AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet", "RuleActionOverrides": [ { "Name": "PHP2Shell_BODY", "ActionToUse": { "Count": {} } }, { "Name": "PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended", "ActionToUse": { "Count": {} } } ] } }, "OverrideAction": { "None": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "AWS-AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet" } }

If PHP2Shell_BODY or PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended matches legitimate requests, keep the rule in Count and add a label-based exception after the rule group. The rule group adds the labels awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body and awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body_Extended to requests that match either rule, and the following rule blocks those requests everywhere except one path. Requests to the excluded path aren’t protected by this rule, so keep the exception as narrow as you can and patch that application first. Labels are case sensitive: confirm the label name in the rule group’s available labels (the DescribeManagedRuleGroup API) before you deploy. For the full pattern, see Creating exceptions in the AWS WAF best practices guide.

{ "Name": "PHP2Shell-Body-Exception", "Priority": 1, "Action": { "Block": {} }, "Statement": { "AndStatement": { "Statements": [ { "OrStatement": { "Statements": [ { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "LABEL", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body" } }, { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "LABEL", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body_Extended" } } ] } }, { "NotStatement": { "Statement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "UriPath": {} }, "PositionalConstraint": "STARTS_WITH", "SearchString": "/path/to/legitimate-upload", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } } } } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBodyException" } }

You can also return a web ACL to Version_2.2 while you tune, but that version includes neither PHP2Shell_BODY nor PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended. Treat a rollback as removing the CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-109618 protection, and prefer the Count override and exception.

PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspect the request body only up to the web ACL body inspection limit. Both use the Continue oversize option, so they don’t inspect content beyond that limit. Pair them with a body size rule such as SizeRestrictions_BODY in the Core rule set (AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet), which blocks request bodies over 8 KB. If you set that rule to Count because of upload paths, use a label-based exception scoped to those paths instead. That keeps the rule in Block everywhere else. For the limit on each resource type, see Request body inspection limits later in this post.

Additional WAF Rules to consider

The managed rule groups cover two of the rules in this section. PHP2Shell_BODY in the PHP application rule group covers CVE-2026-109619, the same CVE as the custom rule later in this post. SizeRestrictions_BODY in the Core rule set caps request bodies at 8 KB, which covers body content beyond the inspection limit. For CVE-2026-109618 itself, the PHP application rule group includes PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended (version 2.4 or later). No AWS managed rule group blocks all multipart requests or rate-limits POST requests, so those two rules remain custom. Use them where they fit your application.

The following rules are in AWS WAF JSON format. Add each one to the protection pack (web ACL) associated with the CloudFront distribution, Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway stage in front of your PHP workloads. Adjust the priorities to fit your web ACL. The AWS WAF best practices guide describes a recommended rule order, with managed rule groups before the label-based exceptions that depend on them.

IMPORTANT: Before you change anything, turn on AWS WAF logging so you can see what each rule matches. Start every rule in Count mode, confirm it doesn’t match legitimate traffic, then switch to Block.

Request body inspection limits The body inspection limit depends on the resource that the web ACL protects. On Application Load Balancer and AWS AppSync, the limit is a fixed 8 KB. On CloudFront, API Gateway, Amazon Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, the default is 16 KB, and you can raise it up to 64 KB through the web ACL AssociationConfig, as shown in the following example. AWS WAF treats any part of the body beyond the limit as oversize. Choose a limit that fits the rules you deploy, because a body size rule can only enforce a cap up to the inspected size.

aws wafv2 update-web-acl ... --association-config \ 'RequestBody={CLOUDFRONT={DefaultSizeInspectionLimit=KB_64}}'

Custom rule for CVE-2026-109619 (if you can’t use the managed rule group) Use this custom rule if you would prefer to use a custom rule instead of a managed rule group. It targets CVE-2026-109619 and blocks a request only when all three conditions in its AndStatement are true at once:

The method is exactly POST, matched on the HTTP method with no transformation.

A PHP session identifier is present (the nested OrStatement, so either sub-condition satisfies this leg):

PHPSESSID appears as a cookie key (exact match on the key, scanning all cookies), or

PHPSESSID appears anywhere in the request body (contains match).

The body contains PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, the form field that activates PHP’s session upload progress feature.

Pair the rule with session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on the server, which turns the feature off. The following rule has its action set to Count. Change it to Block after you confirm it doesn’t match legitimate traffic.

{ "Name": "PHP2Shell", "Priority": 0, "Statement": { "AndStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "POST", "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "OrStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Cookies": { "MatchPattern": { "All": {} }, "MatchScope": "KEY", "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2Shell" } }

Block multipart requests when the application has no uploads

NOTE: This rule, in Block mode, breaks applications that require file uploads. If your application doesn’t require file uploads, blocking removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application for both CVEs at the edge.

AWS WAF inspects a single named header in full, with no 8 KB header limit, so matching the Content-Type header is reliable.

{ "Name": "Block-Multipart-FormData", "Priority": 1, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "SingleHeader": { "Name": "content-type" } }, "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS", "SearchString": "multipart/form-data", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "LOWERCASE" } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockMultipart" } }

Cap the request body size Capping body size reduces the out-of-memory condition behind CVE-2026-109618 and the stale state it can leave behind. It also covers request bodies larger than the inspection limit, which body-inspecting rules such as PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended evaluate only in part. If you use the Core rule set, its SizeRestrictions_BODY rule blocks bodies over 8 KB by default. Use the following custom rule when you need a different threshold or don’t use the Core rule set. It uses OversizeHandling: MATCH with a size constraint so that any body larger than the threshold is blocked, including bodies that exceed the inspection limit. To enforce a cap of N bytes, the web ACL body inspection limit must be at least N.

Note that you can’t cap the numeric Content-Length with a size constraint, because the constraint measures the length of the header value string, not the number it contains. If your application has legitimate large uploads, scope this rule to non-upload paths with an AndStatement on the URI path, or it will break those uploads.

{ "Name": "Block-Oversize-Body", "Priority": 2, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "SizeConstraintStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "MATCH" } }, "ComparisonOperator": "GT", "Size": 8192, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockOversizeBody" } }

NOTE: If a specific managed rule breaks legitimate traffic, override that rule to Count rather than disabling the whole group.

Rate-limit repeated attempts A rate-based rule on POST requests limits how many requests one IP address can send. That lowers the chance of triggering either vulnerability through volume. It also makes the stale-state path harder, because that path needs a producer request and a consumer request to land on the same worker. Set the limit from your normal per-IP POST rate; 100 requests per 60 seconds is a starting point. This rule complements a server setting of pm.max_requests=1, which recycles the worker on each request.

{ "Name": "RateLimit-Posts", "Priority": 3, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "RateBasedStatement": { "Limit": 100, "EvaluationWindowSec": 60, "AggregateKeyType": "IP", "ScopeDownStatement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} }, "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY", "SearchString": "POST", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } } } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellRateLimitPosts" } }

Server-side mitigations that complement AWS WAF

These host and runtime changes address the parts of CVE-2026-109619 that sit below the HTTP layer a WAF inspects, so they fall outside its scope by design. Apply them alongside the AWS WAF rules as the host and runtime layer of your defense.

Upgrade PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, and restart every PHP worker so the new runtime is in use. This is the only complete fix for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These releases don’t fix CVE-2026-115560; see the session.upload_progress.enabled bullet. For PHP 8.1 and earlier, see Fix end-of-life PHP versions.

Address CVE-2026-109618 at the PHP level. Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory, or application setting puts a finite limit back. Keep post_max_size low (8M where the application accepts no uploads, 32M where it does), and keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, not RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

Set fatal_error_backtraces=0 on PHP 8.5 and restart every worker. This disables the setting that stores crash-trace state across a request, one of the confirmed ways the vulnerability is triggered.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. This turns off the upload-tracking feature that’s the other confirmed trigger. Keep it off after you patch: it is also PHP’s mitigation for CVE-2026-115560, which the October 21 releases don’t fix.

Prefer php.ini, FPM pool, or server startup configuration over per-request INI overrides (settings applied per request through .htaccess, php_value, or FastCGI PHP_VALUE). Remove obsolete directives so they don’t raise diagnostic warnings.

Eliminate fatal errors and execution timeouts on attacker-reachable routes, including upload, import, error-page, shutdown, serialization, and extension paths.

Set pm.max_requests=1 if performance allows, so each worker process is recycled after one request, which breaks the link between the request that plants stale data and a later request that would reuse it.

Turn on error logging (log_errors=On, a working error_log, error_reporting=E_ALL) and review your Apache, FPM, or proxy logs for repeated warnings, deprecations, fatal errors, and timeouts on attacker-controlled routes. The absence of errors is not proof of safety.

Fix end-of-life PHP versions

PHP 8.1 and earlier no longer receive updates from the PHP project. Which option you have depends on your version and how you install PHP:

Use a vendor backport. Some Linux distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes for older branches. Check with your vendor.

Apply the PHP source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1. Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team published minimal source backports for these three branches, for people who build PHP from source or don’t have an LTS vendor. Rebuild PHP with the backport, deploy it, and restart every PHP worker. For details, see the PHP security advisory.

Upgrade to a supported release. This is the long-term fix. It’s also the only option for PHP 7.3 and earlier if your vendor doesn’t provide a backport.

A backport fixes these vulnerabilities, but the branch is still end of life and won’t get other security fixes. Treat a backport as a bridge to an upgrade, not a replacement for one. When you upgrade, target PHP 8.3 or later, because PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

For many applications, the upgrade takes code changes as well as a runtime change. Later PHP versions removed language features and extensions that older code often depends on. Plan the upgrade as follows:

Identify each application on PHP 8.1 or earlier, and the frameworks and Composer dependencies it uses.

Review the PHP migration guides for each version between your current release and the target. Update the code, dependencies, and framework versions to match.

Run your tests and static analysis against the target version before you deploy.

Deploy on a fixed release and restart every PHP worker.

One option for implementing the code changes is the AWS Transform PHP version upgrade transformation (AWS/php-version-upgrade, in early access). It upgrades applications from PHP 5.x, 7.x, or 8.0 through 8.4 to PHP 8.5, and it runs your existing tests and static analysis before and after the upgrade. For details, see AWS-managed transformations, or contact your AWS account team.

Until each workload runs a fixed release or a backport, keep the AWS WAF rules and server-side mitigations in this post in place. They reduce exposure, but they don’t fix the vulnerabilities.

Getting started

Complete the following steps to get started:

Inventory where PHP runs and which versions and server APIs (mod_php, FPM, FrankenPHP, LSAPI) are in use. Identify any public endpoint that accepts a request body.

Identify workloads on PHP 8.1 or earlier. Apply a vendor backport or the PHP source backport where one exists, and start the upgrade to a supported release, because it can take longer than a runtime patch. See Fix end-of-life PHP versions.

Check the web ACL in front of each PHP workload. If it uses the PHP application rule group at the default version, PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are already active. If it pins a static version, change it to Version_2.4 or later, or remove the Version field to use the default version.

Add the PHP application rule group and the Core rule set where they’re missing. Then decide whether each application uses multipart uploads, which determines whether you can add the rule that blocks multipart requests.

Add the applicable custom rules in Count mode. Raise the body inspection limit on CloudFront or API Gateway if a rule needs it.

Watch the sampled requests and Amazon CloudWatch metrics for each rule. Confirm that legitimate uploads and large JSON POSTs aren’t matched.

Switch the rules to Block after the metrics are clean. Test the custom rules with a benign multipart/form-data POST, an oversized body, and a POST request that has a PHPSESSID cookie and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in the body. After you switch to Block, expect a 403 response and the matching rule metric.

In parallel, apply the PHP upgrade and the configuration mitigations. Remove or retain the AWS WAF rules as supporting controls after your fleet is patched.

Conclusion

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—are unauthenticated RCE vulnerabilities that reach PHP before your application code runs. AWS WAF gives you a way to help narrow the attack surface during the patch window. Turn on the PHP application managed rule group at the default version (or version 2.4 or later if you pin) and the Core rule set. Then add the custom controls that fit your application: block multipart requests where no uploads are expected, cap request body size, and rate-limit repeated attempts. These mitigating controls can help reduce exposure, but they don’t close the vulnerabilities. If you run PHP 8.1 or earlier, apply a backport where one is available and plan your upgrade to a supported release. If you run PHP 8.2 or later then upgrade PHP to a fixed release, apply the server configuration changes (including session.upload_progress.enabled=0, which also covers CVE-2026-115560 until PHP releases a fix), and treat AWS WAF as the edge layer that supports those fixes rather than the fix itself.

To learn more, see the PHP application managed rule group and the AWS Managed Rules changelog, managed rule group versioning, the web ACL body inspection limit, oversize request component handling, and the AWS re:Post article on handling oversize HTTP request bodies. For tuning and exceptions, see the AWS WAF best practices guide. For the vulnerability details, see the PHP advisories GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp, and the PHP session upload progress manual.

AWS thanks Wiz for reporting the PHP2Shell issues, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, to AWS through coordinated disclosure ahead of their public release. Wiz shared its findings with AWS ahead of publicly disclosing. Using Wiz’s findings, AWS developed and tested AWS WAF managed rules that provide an additional layer of protection for customers who use PHP-based workloads.

AWS values its collaboration with Wiz and the broader security research community. Coordinated disclosure of this kind allows AWS to better prepare protections to help customers in advance of a public disclosure.

articles.title: A patched PHP server can still be a compromised one by Lucie Cardiet
articles.context: Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad...
articles.full_text:
On October 20, details of two critical flaws in PHP leaked online before the fixes were ready. PHP, the scripting language behind a large share of the web, moved its patch release up a day and shipped it on October 21. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed php2shell), let an attacker run commands on a web server through PHP itself, with no login needed.

Patch now. CISA added both flaws to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on October 26. That advice is right, and it leaves a gap. This post is about the gap.

Attackers were testing the flaw before the fix existed

Fixes are out for PHP 8.2 to 8.5,and PHP says PHP 8.1 and older will not get updates. One estimate counts about 884,000 such servers still online, a rough figure from a single source.

Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw early attacks, and the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned organizations to update immediately or take systems offline. How many real servers were taken over is still unclear. Amazon says it does not know whether the attempts it saw would have worked outside a honeypot.

On October 23, CrowdStrike and Flare still reported only probing and failed attempts, many of which crash PHP rather than give an attacker control. The next day, Perplexity's Adel Karimi recorded successful remote code execution on a honeypot, and on October 26 CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, with a federal patch deadline of October 29. Karimi's test used a deliberately favorable setup, so it shows the flaw works, not how often attacks like it succeed.

Every flaw has been out there for a while before anyone announces it

A flaw becomes news on the day it is announced, not the day it appears. PHP's own maintainers first spotted signs of this problem in a 2024 audit, and attackers reached it before the public did.

We have seen this pattern before. When Log4j hit in December 2021, Vectra wrote that the first sign of an attack was hard to spot and that the safest assumption was that at least one server in an estate was already compromised. Other flaws in the software your business runs are very likely in the same position today: known to someone, announced to no one. Patching deals with the ones you hear about. It cannot help with the rest.

The PHP servers you miss matter most

PHP runs WordPress,Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, hosting control panels, and a lot of software that never mentions PHP. The servers you know about will get patched. The ones you do not know about are the ones attackers find first, because nobody is watching them.

Appliances and management interfaces that ship PHP are the likeliest place an attempt becomes a compromise, and they are rarely monitored like web servers. Flare, relaying one researcher's report, says some ship PHP without address randomization, which removes the main obstacle for an attacker. Ask your vendors which of their products include PHP.

No team patches everything on the day a fix ships. Knowing which servers face the internet, and which hold the most valuable data, turns a backlog into a short list of decisions, including which services to switch off until they are fixed. On any server you suspect was hit, save logs and a snapshot of memory before restarting, because a restart erases traces.

‍

What happens after a PHP server falls

An attacker who gets code running through PHP usually does not need malware. The web server already has a shell, a network connection and access to files, so they can use the tools already installed on the machine to look around, find credentials and move from one system to the next. Nothing looks wrong, because the web server is doing web server things with slightly different commands. That is the first of the three detection gaps I write about: nothing looks wrong.

What changes is where the server talks to. A web server that has served the same pages for years suddenly reaches places it never did before, calls out to unfamiliar addresses, or starts talking to internal systems. That behavior shows up in network traffic, not in patch status. A view of the network is how you see what a server is actually connecting to, whether or not anyone is watching the server itself.

What Vectra AI can and cannot see

Vectra AI is not really concerned about what the initial attack vector is. What we see is what happens afterward.

PHP is the story today. Next week it will be something else: another flaw, a phone call to a help desk, someone on the inside. What we look at does not depend on which door was used. We watch what a system does once an attacker is inside, so we do not need the way in to be known or the flaw to be published. That matters most when the entry point is unknown or the vulnerability has not been announced yet.

Uncovering Potential PHP Servers and Shadow IT

One of the challenges in securing PHP infrastructure is knowing where it exists in the first place. Forgotten applications, unmanaged servers, and shadow IT can create security blind spots, even after known vulnerabilities have been patched.

Vectra AI's PHP Server Visibility dashboard provides an additional investigative tool to help security teams identify potentially overlooked PHP servers using indicators observed in unencrypted HTTP traffic, such as .php endpoints and PHPSESSID cookies. Analysts can then investigate whether these hosts are also receiving externally originated encrypted traffic, helping prioritize potentially exposed systems for further investigation.

The dashboard is not intended to provide a complete inventory of PHP servers. It can only identify systems exhibiting observable PHP-related indicators, and encrypted traffic or limited network visibility may leave some servers undiscovered. Instead, it acts as an assistant to existing asset discovery and threat-hunting workflows, helping analysts uncover potential shadow IT, investigate exposure, and identify systems that warrant closer examination, even after patching.

Detection rules for known php2shell exploit attempts

Vectra Match now contains rules to detect the PHP2Shell attacker behaviors when proper visibility is provided to the attacker traffic. They flag known exploit attempts in network traffic when that traffic is visible to us, so they catch attempts at the door, while the detections above catch what follows. An attempt is not a compromise. A match is a reason to look at that server, not proof that it was taken over. This is available for all Vectra Match customers.

The rules, by ET rule number:

2072548: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Handler-mismatch Session Injection (CVE-2026-109619)

2072549: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Header Amplification OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072550: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Nested Empty File Control OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072551: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Chunked Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072552: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Binary URL-Encoded POST for $_POST Corruption (CVE-2026-109618), commented out in the rule set, so off by default

2072553: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072554: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Code Injection in Filename (CVE-2026-109619)

2072555: ET HUNTING PHP Generic Upload Progress Session Manipulation, a hunting rule, not an exploit rule, so treat a match as a lead

2072556: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Multipart Part Count (CVE-2026-109618)

2072557: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Empty Multipart File Controls (CVE-2026-109618)

What a compromised PHP server reveals about your resilience

The old measure of success was whether attackers get in. The better one is how far they get. Patching, a sound network design, splitting the network into zones, least privilege and knowing which systems carry your most important business processes all limit that distance. The network record can show whether anyone came through the door before it closed, and where they went next.

The three gaps are walked end to end in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks white paper.

articles.title: [remote] PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) - PHP core versions after v5.4 - RCE
articles.context: txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab
articles.full_text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3 """PHP2Shell RCE chain for PHP 8.5.11 apache/mod_php. Usage: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --rce 'id>/var/www/html/proof.txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab. Its default endpoint is ``/index.php`` and is configurable with ``--path``. With no ``--rce`` it stops after reproducing the overlong ``Set-Cookie`` disclosure. With ``--rce [COMMAND]`` it composes two distinct PHP memory-safety mechanisms. Bare ``--rce`` runs the documented default and verifies ``/proof.txt``; a custom command is delivered without claiming that its execution was verified. 1. The A1/B1 disclosure is derived from 9bie's cross-request session-state chain. An upload-progress request reaches an OOM bailout before request state is safely reset; a later request in the *same mod_php child* consumes the stale ``PS(id)`` and encodes an attacker-forged ``zend_string`` into the session cookie. This is strongest-fit **CVE-2026-109619** behavior: request- owned session globals outlive their backing request heap. OOM is the producer, but the security boundary crossed by this stage is request lifetime. This is mechanism-based attribution, not a CNA reassignment of any individual public PoC. 2. The optional final sink is adapted from Cookiengineer's OOM RCE. Multipart amplification exhausts the stock 128 MiB heap while ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i()`` has counted but not initialized its final ``HashTable`` bucket. Same-request shutdown walks the incomplete bucket into a forged object, a libphp-only ``jump_fcontext`` ROP chain, and ``zif_system``. This is the incomplete-state/cleanup mechanism of **CVE-2026-109618**. Worker discovery, chunked transfer, prefork saturation, the full-pool scrub, and the clean holder rebind are delivery/affinity techniques, not additional CVEs. The scrub exists because the validated Apache environment can retain children already marked for graceful retirement when its IPv6 listener wakeup fails; without it, a second invocation may place A1 and B1 in different processes. The post-scrub repin is concurrent so VPN latency cannot recreate an idle-surplus window. Debugger mappings were used only to calibrate and independently verify the constants below; successful end-to-end runs derive their live bases from the HTTP cookie. Validated exact environment (2026-10-23) ======================================== This profile is intentionally build-specific. Recalibrate all offsets and heap geometry for any other binary, compiler flags, module set, architecture, or loader layout. * PHP 8.5.11 NTS, Zend Engine 4.5.11, source tag ``php-8.5.11``: annotated tag object ``597eb0b4e32cc8802e112fe13cc92fb5636a1781``; peeled source commit ``678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8``. * Official ``php-8.5.11.tar.xz`` SHA-256: ``d9be75c08e8c316f4c8f4194d8fbe1750a15f6a6d9d4e3fe72082abeeb800360``. * Source build flags: ``-O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fcf-protection=none``; Apache 2.4.66 (Ubuntu) ``mod_php``/prefork on x86-64; glibc 2.43 (Ubuntu ``2.43-2ubuntu2.4``); validation kernel ``Linux 7.0.0-38-generic``. * ``/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so`` SHA-256: ``ecd97e302e8cb3fd106c0541410256ad6597cb6410166beee0ab773ff4974b36``; GNU Build ID ``c01226a7f67b3226c1d2f81f4fc5041846914117``. * ASLR enabled (``kernel.randomize_va_space=2``), Apache defaults including ``StartServers=5`` and ``MaxRequestWorkers=150``, and unmodified upstream ``php.ini-production``: ``memory_limit=128M``, ``post_max_size=8M``, ``upload_max_filesize=2M``, ``max_file_uploads=20``, ``max_input_vars=1000``, ``max_input_nesting_level=64``, error display off, logging on, and session upload progress plus cleanup enabled. * Exact module offsets: ``zval_ptr_dtor=0x7ae960``, ``zif_system=0x598650``, ``jump_fcontext+0x2e=0x6362ae``, ``pop rdi; ret=0x280d8d``, ``pop rsi; ret=0x2cbe07``, and alignment ``ret=0x280d8e``. * Exact heap/layout constants: Zend main chunk ``libphp+0x3400000``; post-disclosure controlled block ``main+0x5c400``; stale-ID forge page ``0x1e3``; 402,500 duplicate multipart headers for the stock-128M sink. * The combined upstream fix used for source comparison is php-src commit ``506e87fa7dcdd306975e5b8f8265ee03527aacbf`` ("Avoid state corruption via bailout"), released in the patched 8.5.12/8.4.27/8.3.30/8.2.29 lines. Recalibrating a different build =============================== Never transplant the constants above based only on ``PHP_VERSION``. Preserve the candidate module first, record its identity, and do all debugger work in an isolated copy of the target environment. For example:: LIBPHP=/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so sha256sum "$LIBPHP" readelf -n "$LIBPHP" | grep 'Build ID' readelf -lW "$LIBPHP" # record executable PT_LOAD ranges nm -an "$LIBPHP" | grep -wE 'zval_ptr_dtor|zif_system|jump_fcontext' ``nm`` values are image-relative because this module is ET_DYN. The pivot is ``jump_fcontext+0x2e`` only after disassembly confirms the same instruction sequence. articles.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot
articles.context: While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains...
articles.full_text:
Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.

The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.

Two lessons from this event apply well beyond this one vulnerability:

An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug. Coordinated disclosure is still the right model. But defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation. With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory.

The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons. In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.

For security leaders, this changes several working assumptions:

For critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours. A 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.

Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17th.

Invest in detections that don’t rely on a signature for a specific CVE. The first exploitation will often come before those signatures exist.

How AWS helps protect customers

AWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.

Immediate recommended actions

Upgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues.

Consider blocking multi-part file uploads in PHP deployments that cannot be patched immediately, but determine how this would affect your application prior to deploying.

Look for POST requests with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS string in form uploads.

Review web server logs for suspicious activity.

Check for unexpected process execution or file modification on web application servers.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)
