The identified IP addresses include shared anonymization infrastructure and are not exclusive to this threat activity. Organizations should investigate any observations involving these addresses as opposed to blocking.

See how to use AWS Web Application Firewall to help reduce your exposure while you patch in our blog post Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

If you have questions, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or reach out to AWS Support.

CJ Moses

CJ Moses is the CISO of Amazon Integrated Security. In his role, CJ leads security engineering and operations across Amazon. His mission is to enable Amazon businesses by making the benefits of security the path of least resistance. CJ joined Amazon in December 2007, holding various roles including Consumer CISO, and most recently AWS CISO, before becoming CISO of Amazon Integrated Security September of 2023.

Prior to joining Amazon, CJ led the technical analysis of computer and network intrusion efforts at the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division. CJ also served as a Special Agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). CJ led several computer intrusion investigations seen as foundational to the security industry today.

CJ holds degrees in Computer Science and Criminal Justice, and is an active SRO GT America GT2 race car driver.

articles.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: PHP Vulnerable to Unauthenticated RCE Attacks
articles.context: *October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours...
articles.full_text: *October 26, 2026: This advisory has been updated to clarify language describing exploitability and potential impact.*October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours following disclosure.IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell,” were publicly disclosed. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. The PHP security team has released emergency patches and strongly encouraged all PHP users to update immediately. These flaws reside in the PHP core language runtime and successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve remote code execution on any server running a vulnerable version, potentially enabling unauthorized access, data theft, or further system compromise. Given PHP's pervasive deployment across web infrastructure globally - including applications like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, as well as embedded devices and similarly overlooked public-facing platforms - the potential attack surface is significant. The vulnerabilities could enable automated exploitation of exposed, vulnerable PHP deployments without authentication or user interaction. The vulnerabilities therefore may be attractive targets for exploitation.ThreatLabz analysis indicates that attackers began rapidly targeting these vulnerabilities following public disclosure, highlighting the need for organizations to patch vulnerable PHP deployments immediately.Zscaler’s security team has analyzed this issue across both production and corporate environments and has ruled out any impact to Zscaler Cloud Platforms, products, distributed components, services, or our enterprise environment, as detailed in the Trust post. RecommendationsOrganizations running PHP should take the following actions:Patch immediately: Upgrade PHP to one of the fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Linux package maintainers received patches in advance and may already have updated packages available. PHP packages for most Linux distributions may also include the patches backported to previous versions of the software, so consult the release notes for your specific installation to ensure your systems are covered.Deactivate unpatched instances: Consider fully disabling services for any PHP instance that cannot be immediately patched. While this may seem overly cautious, any unpatched instance could be targeted by opportunistic adversaries and result in shell-level access to the vulnerable host. Inventory PHP deployments: Conduct an immediate inventory of all PHP installations across your environment, including standalone servers, vendor appliances, bundled software (WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce, Shopware), and hosting panels (cPanel, Plesk, etc).Migrate off EOL branches: Organizations running PHP 5.4+, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1 must migrate to a supported branch immediately. No official binary patches will be released for these versions.Isolate EOL instances that cannot be immediately migrated: Migrating EOL instances is strongly recommended. If this is not possible, isolating unpatchable applications from the internet and other untrusted networks may provide some level of protection. This should be considered a high-risk mitigation and reserved only for business and mission-critical applications while implementing aggressive monitoring of these instances.Monitor for exploitation: Audit web server logs (including but not limited to Apache, Nginx, etc.) for unusual segmentation faults, crash dumps, or abnormal memory usage patterns that may indicate active exploitation attempts.Mitigate risk through PHP settings: While not a definitive fix, mission critical applications that cannot be disabled or immediately patched may benefit from reviewing and tightening memory_limit and max_execution_time settings in php.ini to avoid triggering OOM conditions. Consult additional guidance regarding mitigations through setting session.upload_progress.enabled = Off and disabling multipart uploads at the service edge. ThreatLabz Observes Exploitation Attempts Within 48 HoursThreatLabz observed scanning activity and possible exploitation attempts targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities using multiple attack tools and exploitation methods, including RCE payloads, PHP object injection, and named exploitation frameworks, indicating rapid, in-the-wild exploitation attempts.In the first 48 hours after the PHP2Shell disclosure, Zscaler’s global decoy mesh observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IPs targeting 70 organizations. As a rapid response measure, a new detection rule for PHP2Shell exploitation has been pushed to all Zscaler Deception customers.Attack chainAutomated scanning activity observed by Zscaler suggests attackers may be attempting to use a two-stage PHP2Shell exploitation chain, as shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Notional exploit chain consistent with scanning and exploit attempts observed by ThreatLabz.Stage 1: State setup and fatal triggerThe attacker sends a crafted multipart/form-data POST request containing:A PHPSESSID field to associate the request with a known session, making the session filename (sess_[PHPSESSID]) predictable.The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field to force PHP to begin session bookkeeping during multipart parsing, populating vulnerable global state pointers and writing attacker-controlled data into the session file.A file attachment whose filename= parameter contains either PHP code or a serialized object string.A body sized or structured to exhaust memory (CVE-2026-109618) or trigger a fatal error (CVE-2026-109619).When the fatal condition is triggered, longjmp() aborts the request, freeing per-request memory but leaving stale global pointers.Stage 2: Heap reclaim and code executionThe attacker immediately sends a second request to the same worker process. This second request contains the attacker's payload, sized and aligned to reclaim the freed memory slots. When PHP processes the new request and references the stale global state before re-initialization occurs, it reads and executes the attacker-controlled data, achieving arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker process.Zscaler Deception telemetry findingsThreatLabz observed malicious POST requests targeting the PHP2Shell exploitation path across multiple tools and stages of the attack chain. Every observed request is a multipart/form-data POST targeting PHP endpoints, specifically /, /index.php, /api/endpoint.php, and /app/upload.php.Exploitation payloads observed1. ShellFlow PHP2Shell named exploit toolThe most forensically significant artifact is the presence of a multipart boundary string that explicitly names the exploitation tool. This indicator should not be considered durable, as an adversary can trivially replace the known strings with something less obvious. At this time, the ShellFlow tool uses a known boundary value, so it is a useful indicator for detecting the unmodified tool. The exploit tool request is shown below. POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----shellflow-php2shell ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" sf618_ec172709c8b74601 ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" shellflow_poc ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="poc.bin" Content-Type: application/octet-stream AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA[...15485 bytes total...]The multipart boundary shellflow-php2shell identifies the attacking tool by name. The poc.bin file body contains more than 15k bytes of data along with a repeated AAAA... characters, a characteristic heap spray pattern used for memory layout control in the CVE-2026-109618 OOM corruption path.Notable characteristics:The boundary string shellflow-php2shell directly identifies the ShellFlow PHP2Shell attacking tool, which is publicly linked to CVE-2026-109618 scanning activity.The session ID sf618_ec172709c8b74601 contains sf618, possibly reflecting a developer’s shorthand reference to ShellFlow + CVE-2026-109618.The application/octet-stream upload with a repeating AAAAA... buffer is consistent with a heap spray technique used to influence the memory layout when the OOM condition is triggered.2. Active system() command execution payloadThese requests represent the strongest indication of automated exploitation attempts. The filename= field contains a fully formed PHP webshell instruction designed to be written into the PHP session file through the session.upload_progress handler and later executed, as shown in the example below.The filename= value [?php system('echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt');echo 'RCE';?] instructs the PHP runtime to:Execute the OS command echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt, writing a proof-of-compromise marker to disk.Echo the string RCE in the HTTP response body, providing an indication of successful code execution to the attacker. The RCE string may still be returned even if the preceding echo redirection fails.This payload pattern was observed in two separate requests with identical content, consistent with automated retry behavior commonly seen in exploit frameworks.3. PHP object injection via pipe delimiterThreatLabz also observed a PHP object injection request that abuses the session pipe delimiter, as shown in the example. The filename x|O:8:"stdClass":0:{} uses the PHP default session serialization format, where the | character separates a variable name from its serialized value.POST /app/upload.php HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=--NeoMM2026 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" neosc4n00000000000000002 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" neo_obj_inject --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="x|O:8:\"stdClass\":0:{}" Content-Type: text/plain Z --NeoMM2026--Overall attack tool fingerprinting summaryThreatLabz identified multiple distinct attacker toolsets through analysis of numerous requests in our telemetry, as summarized in the table below:Tool / FrameworkIdentifying MarkersShellFlow PHP2ShellBoundary shellflow-php2shell; session ID prefix sf618; poc.bin heap sprayActive RCE OperatorBoundary --VERIFY; system() payload in filename=; pwned.txt writeNuclei CVE TemplatesBoundary prefix ------Nuclei; echo-test random token in filenameNeo ScannerBoundary --NeoMM2026b / --NeoMM2026; targets /api/endpoint.php, /app/upload.phpTable 1: Attacker tools and identifying markers observed in PHP2Shell exploitation activity. Affected VersionsAll PHP versions from 5.4 onward are vulnerable. Only currently supported branches received patches, but package maintainers may also backport the security patches to previous versions. Carefully review the instructions and release notes from the maintainers of your PHP installations to determine what version and release includes the necessary patch.PHP BranchVulnerable VersionsPatch AvailablePHP 8.58.5.0 – 8.5.11Yes (8.5.12)PHP 8.48.4.0 – 8.4.26Yes (8.4.27)PHP 8.38.3.0 – 8.3.35Yes (8.3.36)PHP 8.28.2.0 – 8.2.34Yes (8.2.35)PHP 8.1All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 8.0All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 7.xAll versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 5.4+All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)Table 2: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Affected PHP Versions and Patch Availability How It WorksBoth vulnerabilities are use-after-free memory safety flaws in PHP's core request-handling engine. All PHP installations serving web requests may be affected regardless of security controls. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory; that memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.CVE-2026-109618: OOM Corruption / Uninitialized Memory UseCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: PHP uses longjmp() to abort a request when it hits its configured memory limit. When a web application receives form input, PHP records new entries in its internal POST data structure before finishing their initialization. If an out-of-memory (OOM) error fires while internal request data is only partially initialized, longjmp() bypasses normal control flow, leaving memory in an inconsistent/uninitialized state. During request cleanup, PHP misinterprets this invalid data as valid and follows an attacker-controlled code pointer, yielding control of execution.Exploit Vector: An attacker can intentionally trigger specific OOM conditions (e.g., via large memory allocations, deeply recursive calls, or maliciously crafted request payloads) to corrupt state and achieve unauthenticated RCE.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code ExecutionCVE-2026-109619: Use-After-Free / Stale Memory AccessCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: When PHP encounters a fatal error and calls zend_bailout() (via longjmp()), request-owned internal state can survive in global memory after its backing allocation has been freed. PHP workers process multiple requests in sequence, and certain internal pointers persist between requests. If a request crashes or exhausts memory at the right moment, those pointers are left pointing to already-recycled memory. A subsequent request processed by the same worker may access this stale memory before re-initialization occurs.Exploit Vector: This vulnerability is chainable with CVE-2026-109618. The partial initialization in CVE-2026-109618 allows an attacker to shape the freed memory contents and gain control of the instruction pointer, potentially enabling RCE. Chaining these two CVEs requires no authentication and no user interaction.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution and memory/credential disclosure ConclusionPHP2Shell represents a significant security issue because of the severity of the vulnerabilities and PHP’s broad deployment. The combination of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 could provide an unauthenticated path to RCE and potentially broader server compromise without user interaction.Organizations are strongly urged to treat this as an emergency patching event. Systems running EOL PHP branches must be migrated without delay. Where patching cannot be completed immediately, network-layer controls should be applied as an interim measure.ThreatLabz will continue to monitor active exploitation campaigns and update Zscaler platform protections as new indicators emerge. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows the typical attack stages and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler.Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and fix any vulnerable PHP applications with Zscaler Exposure ManagementEliminate externally exposed PHP assets by leveraging a Zero Trust architecture.Prevent compromiseDetonate unknown second-stage payloads with Advanced Cloud Sandbox.Route server egress through ZIA to detect/block post-compromise activity.Enable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Enable Advanced Threat Protection to block known C2 domains.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall, to extend C2 controls across all ports/protocols, including emerging C2.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app segmentation for crown-jewel apps (employees and third parties).Use ZPA inline inspection to block exploitation attempts against private apps from compromised users.Use Zscaler Deception to detect and contain lateral movement or privilege escalation with decoy assets and accounts.Use Zscaler MDR and Threat Hunting to detect and respond to early stage threat activity.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler DLP. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with the following signatures:Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionThe Zscaler Advanced Threat Protection signatures detect exploitation attempts from ZIA traffic targeting internet-exposed servers:PHP.Exploit.CVE-2026-109618_19Zscaler Private Access AppProtectionThe ZPA App Protection signatures detect exploitation attempts against internal applications through ZPA, including activity originating from compromised endpoints or insiders:6000568: PHP Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)6000569: PHP2Shell Excessive Multipart Parts (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Zscaler Deception Zscaler Deception customers can deploy Private Threat Intelligence decoys for the following applications to detect PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and generate high-fidelity alerts:WordPress LoginDrupal Admin PanelJoomla Admin PanelphpMyAdminNextcloudCustomers can configure an orchestration rule to add any IP addresses interacting with these decoys to a firewall block list.Zscaler MDRZscaler MDR's behavioral detection analytics also provide generic coverage for this class of web application RCE. The following active detection analytics are candidates for identifying post-exploitation activity that may result from these vulnerabilities:NIX-WEBSERVER-SPAWN-SUSPICIOUS-COMMAND — Linux web servers spawning suspicious commands including reconnaissance utilities and downloadersNIX-WEBSERVER-SPAWN-RECON — Web servers spawning reconnaissance commandsPSX-WEBSERVER-CREATE-PHP-SCRIPT — Web servers creating inline PHP scripts in web directories Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Zscaler Deception observed IP addresses delivering PHP2Shell-related payloads. articles.title: Arctic Wolf Labs: Finding, Prioritizing, and Patching PHP2Shell Exposure
articles.context: On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race...
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race between defenders and attackers. The flaws are tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together they’re known as PHP2Shell. Both carry a 9.2 rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 scale. For both vulnerabilities, Arctic Wolf’s Aurora® Agentic SOC helps organizations rapidly identify affected assets, correlate exploitation signals across the environment, and accelerate investigation and response before attackers can establish persistence.

An unauthenticated attacker can use either flaw to run code on a vulnerable server. On Wednesday, October 21, the PHP project released patched versions. PHP2Shell shows how AI is changing the threat landscape. Attackers can now find and weaponize old flaws in widely used technology faster than ever before. Arctic Wolf recommends treating every PHP installation that serves web requests as at-risk presently. Internet-facing Linux web servers without endpoint monitoring carry the highest risk of quiet compromise.

Patching remains the recommended remediation. Security teams should assess exposure immediately, identify likely attack paths, and segment critical systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment. If attackers exploit PHP2Shell, Aurora Agentic SOC is designed to detect the activity that follows, including webshell deployment, unauthorized command execution, persistence attempts, and lateral movement, enabling rapid investigation and response before attacks can escalate.

Overview and Impact

All PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk. That includes PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates the risk highest for mod_php. In PHP’s demonstrated exploit, an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, and control panels like cPanel and Plesk. Many vendor applications bundle PHP without saying so, which makes the affected assets hard to find. Bundled standalone binaries such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe on Windows are easy to miss.

Understanding the Root Cause

CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. PHP can stop while internal request data is only partly set up. Request cleanup may then treat that invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale state flaw. Request-owned internal state can survive after its memory is freed. A later request on the same worker may use that stale state before normal setup resets it. The PHP session upload progress feature is one confirmed path to this flaw, and it’s enabled by default.

Guidance for Arctic Wolf Customers

Inventory every system that runs PHP. Include package-based installs, containers, appliances, and hosting panels. Include vendor software that bundles PHP. Include continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) images.

Identify the PHP branch and package source on each system.

Update to the patched version or confirm your vendor has backported both fixes. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Restart every affected service. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache, NGINX upstream pools, application workers, and containers.

Rebuild container images from patched upstream bases. Patching only the running containers leaves the image exposed.

Move end-of-life PHP to a supported branch.

Record the patched version, vendor advisory, restart time, and validation evidence for each host or image. If a workload can’t be patched right away, document compensating controls and an approved exception with an expiry date.

Patched versions

PHP branch

Support status

Patched version

Action

8.5

Active support

8.5.12

Update immediately

8.4

Active support

8.4.27

Update immediately

8.3

Security fixes only

8.3.36

Update immediately

8.2

Security fixes only

8.2.35

Update immediately, then plan an upgrade

8.1 and older

End-of-life

None from the PHP project

Upgrade or get fixes from your vendor

The PHP project no longer releases updates for 8.1 or older. Some distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes, so check with your vendor.

Audit commands

Use these commands to find PHP packages and confirm that your vendor backported both fixes.

Platform

Command

Ubuntu or Debian

dpkg -l | grep php

Ubuntu or Debian

apt changelog php8.3-cli | grep -E “CVE-2026-109618|CVE-2026-109619”

rpm -qa | grep php

RHEL, Rocky Linux, or AlmaLinux

rpm -q php-cli –changelog | grep -E “CVE-2026-109618|CVE-2026-109619”

Alpine containers

apk info | grep php

Use stopgaps to reduce exposure while you patch

Configuration changes such as memory_limit or session.upload_progress.enabled are not remediation. PHP states that only an update is a complete solution. The required fix is a patched PHP runtime or a vendor package that explicitly backports both fixes.

If you can’t update right away, PHP lists measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths. These measures do not make an installation safe.

For CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration.

Set a low post_max_size. PHP suggests 8M for applications without uploads and 32M for those with uploads. Keep upload_max_filesize below it.

Enforce request size, field count, and header limits at the web server or proxy.

Skip RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA because they can trigger the vulnerable allocation failure.

For CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or in an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Then restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts.

How Arctic Wolf Labs turns telemetry into outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global SOC telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base. Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This means customers gain coverage against PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance

As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments. Arctic Wolf Labs’ initial investigation has identified numerous scanning efforts as well as malicious exploitation attempts, including passing wget requests to retrieve both ELF and Golang binaries associated with commodity malware.

How the Aurora Superintelligence Platform keeps customers protected

The Aurora Superintelligence Platform helps organizations reduce PHP2Shell risk before and after exploitation. Aurora Vulnerability Management identifies and prioritizes affected assets using live exploit activity and threat intelligence, helping security teams focus remediation efforts where risk is highest.

PHP2Shell vulnerability detections in Aurora Vulnerability Management

The Aurora Agentic SOC monitors the behaviors attackers rely on after exploitation, including webshell deployment, suspicious processes spawned by PHP or web servers, malicious command execution, persistence activity, and lateral movement.

Together, these capabilities help organizations quickly identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation, detect malicious activity, investigate potential compromise, and contain threats while vulnerable systems are being patched. As the threat evolves, Arctic Wolf continuously incorporates new intelligence across the platform to strengthen proactive cyber risk remediation and detection and response capabilities for all customers.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: How to Protect Vulnerable PHP Workloads While Patching
articles.context: Aquasec provides vulnerability detection and runtime controls to help identify exposure and restrict supported unauthorized activities while customers apply security updates
articles.full_text:
How does Aquasec protect PHP workloads?

Aquasec enforces security policies inside running workloads, allowing security teams to restrict supported unauthorized actions without depending exclusively on vulnerability specific signatures.

Four runtime control areas are particularly relevant to PHP workloads.

Restrict unauthorized process execution. Runtime policies can restrict PHP workloads from launching unnecessary shells and download utilities such as `sh`, `bash`, `curl` and `wget`. This can interrupt certain attempts to execute additional commands or retrieve malicious payloads.

Prevent unauthorized executable changes. Aquasec Drift Prevention can block execution of executable files that were not present in the original container image. This helps restrict newly introduced malicious binaries, although it does not independently prevent a PHP script from running through the existing interpreter.

Restrict unauthorized network activity. Appropriate runtime network controls can restrict unnecessary outbound connections and help limit certain reverse shell activities or communication with attacker controlled infrastructure.

Protect application files. File integrity monitoring can detect unauthorized modifications to sensitive application directories. File modification restrictions can prevent changes when properly configured, including changes to PHP web roots where malicious scripts might be introduced.

The effectiveness of these controls depends on workload coverage, policy configuration and the attack technique. In enforcement mode, validated policies can block supported unauthorized actions. They should not be represented as complete protection against either PHP2Shell vulnerability, particularly the reported memory disclosure path.

articles.title: Limits of Java Certificate Bypass: Fingerprint Blocklist Insights
articles.context: TL;DR Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked
articles.full_text:
TL;DR

Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked.certs rejected the listed certificate encodings but accepted re-encoded versions that still validated in the tested configurations.

We reproduced the behavior with ECDSA- and RSA-signed intermediates associated with the eMudhra incident. Each re-encoded certificate had a different SHA-256 fingerprint.

The results apply to the JDK versions and trust-store configurations tested. Follow current vendor guidance and verify the protections in the runtimes and trust stores you deploy.

A certificate blocklist can reject a known-bad certificate and still miss another encoding of it.

We saw this while examining Java's response to the eMudhra certificate incident. The mitigation uses SHA-256 fingerprints to identify compromised intermediate certificates. But a certificate’s fingerprint is calculated from its exact encoded bytes.

During an AI-assisted review, Sonatype Research Labs asked Opus 5.5 whether Java's exact-fingerprint blocking could be bypassed. The AI model flagged that exact-byte matching might leave room for equivalent certificate encodings.

We confirmed the behavior for both ECDSA and RSA certificates: re-encoded intermediates had different SHA-256 fingerprints, yet still validated in our Java trust-store tests. This points to a limit in exact-fingerprint blocking: it can identify the certificate bytes it knows about without necessarily covering every equivalent encoding.

Here, we’ll explain how the re-encoding works, what the tests show, and what teams should check before relying on a certificate blocklist as their only mitigation.

How It Started: eMudhra Certificates Compromised

Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authority keys were compromised on October 20, 2026, allowing anyone who obtained a key to create certificates that could be trusted as part of a chain to a trusted root. Browser and platform vendors responded with blocks and trust-store changes.

This also prompted a Java mitigation: add the affected intermediates to blocked.certs. Our research began with a narrower question: does that fingerprint-based block reject every valid encoding of those certificates?

How Exact-Fingerprint Blocking Works

A certificate is a structured document: it contains information such as the subject, public key, issuer, validity period, and a digital signature. In Java, blocked.certs identifies certificates by their SHA-256 fingerprints. The fingerprint is calculated from the certificate's encoded bytes, so even a small change to those bytes produces a different fingerprint.

This makes fingerprint blocking precise, but the match depends on the exact encoding in the blocklist. If a certificate can be re-encoded and still pass signature validation, the new encoding may have a different fingerprint and may not match the listed entry. To test whether an alternate encoding could still validate in practice, we examined two signature formats: ECDSA and RSA.

Changing the Encoding Changes the Result

We tested two certificate chains from the eMudhra incident advisory: one with an ECDSA-signed intermediate and one with an RSA-signed intermediate. For each, the reproduction added the original intermediate's SHA-256 fingerprint to a copy of a JDK's blocked.certs file, changed the intermediate's encoding without its private key, then checked whether the chain still validated.

The two encoding changes were:

ECDSA: The script changes the signature value from s to n − s, another valid representation of the signature.

RSA: It removes the NULL parameter from the outer signature algorithm identifier. The signature over the certificate data remains unchanged.

Both tests produced the same result:Java rejected the original chain whose intermediate fingerprint was listed, but trusted the chain with the re-encoded intermediate, whose fingerprint was different. After the relevant roots were removed from the copied JDK’s trust store, both chains were rejected.

Verify the Mitigation in Your Runtime

Teams should verify certificate mitigations in the Java runtimes and trust stores they deploy. Removing the relevant roots rejected both chains in our tests, but it can also interrupt legitimate TLS connections. Before changing a trust store, identify dependent services, test their certificate chains, and monitor for TLS failures after deployment.

Follow current vendor guidance and document any exceptions. These results cover only the JDK versions and trust-store configurations we examined, so validate the controls separately for other runtimes and TLS paths in your environment.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Makes PHP Inventory and Patch Ownership Urgent
articles.context: As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet
articles.full_text:
Updated October 23, 2026: PHP disclosed a related follow-on issue, CVE-2026-115560, involving an unlikely remote code execution (RCE) vector under unusual session settings. PHP recommends disabling session.upload_progress.enabled until the next regular bugfix release. See our research and recommendation in Sonatype Guide for more details.

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is the name being used for two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

PHP says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, with the highest risk in Apache configurations using mod_php. Fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Organizations should inventory PHP across their environments, prioritize internet-facing systems, monitor for suspicious activity, and apply the update through PHP or the relevant distribution or product vendor. If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

On October 23, 2026, PHP disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate follow-on RCE issue. Temporarily disable session.upload_progress.enabled as PHP recommends, then apply the complete PHP fix when available.

PHP2Shell Is Two Critical Flaws in the PHP Runtime

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP's internal request handling. Because PHP is used in websites, applications, and products, affected installations may be managed by different teams or supplied through different vendors.The urgent work is to find those systems, establish who owns each one, and verify that the fix reaches every deployment.

Sonatype's PHP2Shell Security Event tracks current guidance and response recommendations.

CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory handling: PHP may interrupt a request while internal data is only partly initialized, then handle that data incorrectly during cleanup.

CVE-2026-109619 involves a stale global state that can persist after its underlying memory has been freed.

PHP says CVE-2026-115560 can occur when an application configures session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, switches it to php at runtime before calling session_start(), and leaves session upload progress enabled. PHP had already listed disabling upload progress as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619. This setting does not cover every affected path, and that a PHP release containing the complete state-reset patch is the reliable remediation.

Under affected conditions, the flaws can allow a remote attacker to execute code without authentication.

Ilkka Turunen, Sonatype's Field CTO, puts the operational priority plainly: "The immediate priority is clear accountability: know where PHP is used across your services and products, who owns remediation, and how quickly fixes can be deployed."

The Hard Part Is Finding Every PHP Installation

Organizations may know that their public websites use PHP but have less visibility into internal portals, older services, appliances, or software that bundles its own runtime. Different teams may also install and maintain PHP through separate operating system distributions, hosting providers, or third-party vendors.

Turunen expects remediation to extend beyond visible websites and services. PHP is bundled into other products and remains in older environments, creating what he calls "a long tail of environments needing to apply this patch."

A complete response starts with an inventory that connects each runtime to an owner and a patch path. Teams should identify:

Which internet-facing and internal systems run PHP.

The PHP version and how it is supplied or maintained.

Which applications, containers, images, appliances, and products include a PHP runtime.

The business or service owner responsible for remediation.

Whether a fixed package is available from PHP, the operating system distributor, hosting provider, or another vendor.

Include systems that are easy to overlook: older applications with little traffic, test environments that remain reachable, and deployments maintained outside the central platform team. An incomplete inventory can make an organization believe remediation is finished while vulnerable installations remain online.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. PHP says some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported fixes, and it has also published source backports for selected older branches. Organizations using these versions should confirm the status with their distribution or vendor, or plan an upgrade to a supported release. Do not assume an upstream version number alone tells you whether a vendor-maintained package includes the fix.

Patch, Verify, and Monitor Across the Estate

PHP says updating to a fixed release is the only complete solution. Temporary controls can reduce exposure to specific attack paths, and a web application firewall can add protection for traffic routed through it. Cloudflare reported deploying protections and seeing attack traffic aimed at its customers, while urging users to patch.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, the UK National Cyber Security Centre advises organizations to consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated. If it must remain available, assign an owner and document interim protections and a reassessment date.

The discovery and response also highlight the role AI is playing in vulnerability research. The Wall Street Journal reported that Calif and Wiz researchers used AI tools during a PHP source-code audit, and that developers, researchers, and distributors coordinated on fixes after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure.

As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet."

What Organizations Should Do Now

PHP2Shell is a test of whether organizations can find, own, and update the software running across their environments. PHP has published fixes, but a release only reduces risk when the update reaches every affected runtime, including those inside products and services maintained by other vendors.

Organizations should:

Inventory systems running PHP, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Monitor internet-facing PHP systems for suspicious activity.

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or apply the relevant vendor backport. Include products and services that bundle PHP.

Check PHP, distribution, and third-party vendor advisories for updates, especially when running PHP 8.1 or older.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

For ongoing details and links to current advisories, see the official PHP security advisory.

Written by Sonatype Research Team

Sonatype's Research Team is focused on bringing real-time, in-depth intelligence and actionable information about open source and third party vulnerabilities to Sonatype customers.

Explore All Posts by Sonatype Research Team

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.context: Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in PHP
articles.context: Overview On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP
articles.full_text:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges.

CVE

CVSSv4

Description

CVE-2026-109618

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via OOM corruption

CVE-2026-109619

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via stale global state

All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs.

The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon.

Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles.

Multiple public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are now available. Rapid7 researchers have reviewed these and observe that each demonstrates RCE only against a specific combination of operating system, PHP version, and web server, and none appears to be broadly reliable. Rapid7’s own research supports this. Our attempts so far have produced a working exploit only under narrow lab conditions, and exploitation depends on assumptions that are unlikely to hold on internet-facing instances. We are continuing to investigate approaches that could improve portability, but have not yet developed a reliable, general-purpose exploit. Rapid7 has not observed exploitation in the wild, though there are multiple reports of exploitation attempts, which is expected for a vulnerability of this profile. The situation is evolving quickly, and a more portable exploit technique could emerge at any time. The current difficulty of reliable exploitation should be treated as a window to patch rather than a reason to delay, and Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis.

Update #1: On October 26, 2026, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA set the remediation due date to October 29, 2026, for affected Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies and directs them to follow the associated BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements. Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis and investigating for prior compromise.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling

According to the OOM advisory, PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM.

Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. The advisory reports RCE over HTTP with default PHP input and memory limits, including multi-worker prefork deployments. PHP-FPM terminates a worker when startup fails, preventing that particular sequence. Source analysis supports FPM susceptibility after successful startup, but the advisory reports no complete FPM exploit for this CVE. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior, and memory layout.

CVE-2026-109619: Use after free across requests

PHP can reuse a worker process to handle multiple HTTP requests. The stale-state advisory describes internal state that still points to memory freed at the end of an earlier request. A later request handled by the same worker can access that stale value before normal initialization clears it. Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset.

The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start().

The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition.

Mitigation guidance

PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions:

PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35

PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36

PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27

PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement, or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source.

Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation.

PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment:

For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit.

For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern.

Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length. If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP.

Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path.

For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting, display_errors, log_errors, or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe.

For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and stale global state advisory.

Rapid7 customers

To learn how to use Rapid7 capabilities to find systems affected by these vulnerabilities and for answers to common questions, read the PHP2Shell documentation.

For Rapid7 Customers with questions regarding Rapid7 products and their usage of PHP please consult this page.

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with remote unauthenticated vulnerability checks, available in a dedicated release that followed the regular October 21 content release.

Rapid7 has also released authenticated scan checks for both the Scan Engine and the Agent for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as part of the October 22 content release.

Authenticated, package-based checks are now available for a variety of Linux distributions. These checks evaluate installed distribution packages, so they can recognize backported fixes that keep the original upstream PHP version number. Run an authenticated scan with this content release to use them. For the full list of checks and supported distribution versions, read Rapid7’s PHP2Shell documentation, where package-based coverage for other distributions will be added as their fixes are published.

In a dedicated October 23 content release following the regular release, Rapid7 has released coverage for CVE-2026-115560, published on October 23 by the PHP Foundation. A mitigation technique is available, but no patch has yet been published. Exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 relies on non-standard configuration.

Current scope for authenticated coverage: Windows, macOS and Linux. Remote unauthenticated coverage provides coverage regardless of web-server OS.

Velociraptor

A Velociraptor Artifact Generic.Applications.PHPInventory is available to inventory PHP installations on Windows, Linux and macOS for remediation scoping. This artifact allows for the collection of package versions, common binary and module paths, and running PHP processes.

Updates

October 21, 2026: Initial publication.

October 21, 2026: Updated to reflect availability of vulnerability checks.

October 22, 2026: Updated the Overview section to include Rapid7’s findings on a PoC and the Rapid7 Customers section to include a link to the FAQ documentation.

October 23, 2026: Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to describe authenticated coverage, Linux distro backported coverage, and more.

October 27, 2026: Updated the Overview to note that CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to the CISA KEV catalog. Updated Rapid7 customers section to reflect added Windows support.

articles.title: “Next Exploit Opportunities”: How a Threat Actor Used AI to Help Plan and Execute Multiple Types of Cybercrime Activities
articles.context: Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks...
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

“Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing [sic],” the threat actor typed. The conversation was with one of several AI assistants that the actor was using to get advice on planning and executing a variety of cybercrime activities.

Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks across multiple campaign types.

Unit 42’s investigation into the actor’s operational environment and activities makes two things clear:

The attacker used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, suggesting they didn’t have the skills these activities would have required before the advent of readily available AI tools.

Despite some apparent bumbling, the actor had an impact, attacking a number of targets in India, including universities. The actor recovered thousands of records revealing personal information and mapped multiple organizations’ attack surfaces.

The attacker’s conversations with jailbroken AI tools included getting step by step advice on how to set up a fraudulent Voice over IP (VoIP) operation. One assistant “helpfully” generated a document including a “NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES” section, outlining planned followup attacks.

Unit 42 identified and investigated this threat actor's operational environment. There, we determined that they had weaponized an AI assistant across several types of cybercrime, including:

Credential theft and data exfiltration

VoIP telecommunications fraud

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

Command-and-control (C2) operations

An actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) as a secondary tool, both with safety controls disabled. The actor ran an AI-generated brute-force campaign against an Indian university’s website. The actor also achieved a confirmed intrusion against a second university, where they exfiltrated a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students.

The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders). Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Multiple, unrelated actors are independently adopting the same Hermes + DeepSeek combination. This suggests we may be witnessing an increasingly prevalent toolchain of choice for cybercriminals adopting AI-enabled capabilities. We assess a key driver is low safety friction at low cost: DeepSeek models are inexpensive and easy to access, and readily jailbroken with a simple system-prompt override.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced IP Defense

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Cortex Cloud

Idira Privileged Access Manager (PAM)

Idira Identity and Access Manager (IAM)

Idira Secrets Manager

The Unit 42 AI Security Assessment and Unit 42 Frontier AI Defense service can help identify and mitigate complex AI-enabled risks.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

AI, Credential Theft, Cryptocurrency

Technical Analysis

We identified evidence that the threat actor leveraged AI systems for a wide range of criminal activity against multiple target networks, primarily in India. The criminal activity included:

Planning for VoIP fraud

Credential theft targeting several organizations

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

C2 payloads

Credential Theft and Data Exfiltration

WordPress Brute Force

The actor used AI-generated reconnaissance to conduct a methodical attack against an Indian university's online education platform. The actor’s enumeration reports exhibit structured formatting (executive summaries, severity ratings, systematic endpoint categorization) consistent with AI-generated output. The attack progressed through four stages:

Subdomain enumeration: The actor identified 12 subdomains including the main WordPress site, a learning management system (LMS), student portal and administration dashboard

WordPress REST API enumeration: The actor extracted 13 active user IDs with real names via post author fields and author sitemaps, bypassing the Cloudflare Web Application Firewall (WAF) that blocked direct user endpoint access

Targeted brute force: A generator script produced a brute force tool with 117 usernames (derived from the enumeration) and 28 common passwords

Credential brute force: The actor’s tool flagged one WordPress login as valid

Figure 1 shows an excerpt from the actor's WordPress REST API enumeration report (stage 2).

Figure 2 shows output from a brute force attempt that recorded a candidate credential (stage 4).

University Database Exfiltration

The actor exfiltrated a MongoDB database from a second Indian public university. The exfiltration tooling wrote a manifest alongside the dumped collections, recording the following data:

Admin credential obtained: An administrator account with a weak password

Exfiltrated records: Thousands of student records (diploma, undergraduate, postgraduate) and faculty records containing PII

Infrastructure exposed: Cloud load balancing, edge routing, database services, and a third-party cloud storage service account

E-Commerce Enumeration

The actor enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform, extracting:

A storefront API token

Three admin email addresses

Two phone numbers

Payment merchant IDs

The attack report is a suspected large language model (LLM)-generated document, including a NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES section outlining planned follow-up attacks.

VoIP Telecommunications Fraud

We also identified evidence that the actor was developing VoIP (Voice over IP) fraud infrastructure, using the alice Hermes profile as an AI-powered advisor. Evidence included:

Advisory conversations

A detailed technical knowledge base

Carrier research

However, the absence of call logs, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) traces or active call routing suggested the operation was still in a planning or early setup phase.

With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, alice provided detailed, actionable criminal methodology through conversations and a comprehensive fraud knowledge base ingested into the bot. The actor developed a planned approach following an established VoIP fraud model:

Establish a legitimate front: Register a US limited liability company (LLC) with an employer identification number (EIN) to qualify as a telecommunications provider. The knowledge base includes detailed guidance on:

Forming LLCs in Wyoming or Delaware as a non-US resident

Obtaining an EIN without a Social Security number via the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) fax

Completing Federal Communications Commission (FCC) registration

Obtain carrier access: Contract with legitimate VoIP carriers to purchase call routing capacity (SIP trunks).

Traffic mixing: Route approximately 70% legitimate call traffic alongside 30% fraudulent calls to stay below carrier compliance audit thresholds.

Bypass caller ID authentication: Circumvent STIR/SHAKEN, the FCC-mandated caller identity verification framework. In the advisory conversations, alice covers bypass techniques and Calling Line Identification (CLI) spoofing.

Monetize: Generate revenue with the 30% fraudulent traffic through toll fraud and other non-compliant routes. Least-cost routing (LCR) optimizes per-minute costs across carrier tiers.

Figure 3 shows an excerpt from an alice conversation including the actor asking and DeepSeek advising on fraud traffic ratios and carrier evasion.

The pandarouter profile handled carrier research. The excerpt below in Figure 4 illustrates how the actor used it to investigate a wholesale VoIP carrier for regulatory vulnerabilities and past fraud.

Other Operations

Command and Control

The threat actor’s infrastructure maintained a listening port for a Python-based C2 listener supporting Windows reverse shell connections. Supporting payloads include:

A Base64-encoded PowerShell reverse shell delivered via VBScript

A QubesOS VM setup script with SSH and ncat

Multiple Windows shell variants

Wi-Fi Password Cracking

The actor developed an automated Wi-Fi password cracking process. A Linux (Kali) device the actor labeled Pi placed within range of target Wi-Fi networks captured Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) authentication material (PMKID or EAPOL handshakes) from nearby access points.

The server collected these hashes over an SSH tunnel and dispatched them to Vast.ai cloud GPU instances for cracking, with results automatically reported back to the actor via Discord webhooks. This technique requires physical proximity to the target networks, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Credential Scanning Toolkit

We also identified a large Go-based credential-scanning toolkit. This toolkit scrapes webpages and extracts exposed credentials, including:

.env values

S3 signed URLs

Google Cloud service account keys

Content delivery network (CDN) API keys

Private keys in log files

A companion Python script scrapes domain lists for scanning.

Cryptocurrency Reconnaissance

The actor scraped the top 500 ETH holders and major token holders via the DeBank API, producing intelligence files that documented 45 cryptocurrency whales with net worth figures. We assess this was likely for future targeting, but we were unable to identify any follow-on activity during this research.

Tool Design and Infrastructure

The threat actor used a single US-based server (162.243.3[.]92) to host multiple core services, including:

The Hermes Agent framework

A C2 listener

A Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) proxy

Several supporting components

Our analysis of the actor’s logs and test scripts indicates that they experimented with various LLMs, including GLM 5.2 by Zhipu AI and other models accessed through OpenRouter. Ultimately, they chose DeepSeek V4 as the backend for operations.

The actor's test scripts show repeated attempts to defeat model safety controls with a prompt-level override. Although GLM 5.2 is an open-weight model that has been reported as weakly guarded, the actor built a dedicated script to send the override to GLM 5.2 and flag refusals. This is evidence of resistance the actor worked to overcome.

The actor ultimately operationalized DeepSeek V4, consistent with the minimal safety controls observed in the Chinese-speaking activity we previously reported. Figure 5 shows an example of the system prompt the actor used to override model safety controls (from the actor's model-testing scripts, e.g., test_batch1.py).

Table 1 summarizes the actor's AI tool configurations.

Tool

Model

Role

Safety Configuration

Hermes Agent

DeepSeek V4

Primary AI assistant, Telegram-controlled

System prompt override

Cursor IDE

Multiple models configured (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Composer 2.5, others)

AI-assisted code generation

Agent mode forced and permission checks bypassed via proxy environment variables; IDE sandbox set to disabled; MCP servers auto-approved

Table 1. AI tool configurations.

Figure 6 shows a flowchart that illustrates the actor's infrastructure and how the AI tools interconnect.

The Hermes Agent served as the actor's primary interface, controlled via Telegram direct messages. The actor maintained three Hermes profiles as specialized AI modes, each running as a separate Telegram bot gateway spawned from the operator's session (Table 2).

Profile

Command

Working Directory (CWD)

Description

make-good

hermes gateway run --profile make-good

General-purpose criminal assistant with safety overrides

alice

hermes gateway run --profile alice

VoIP fraud advisor; covers carrier compliance evasion, STIR/SHAKEN bypass and LLC formation

pandarouter

hermes gateway run --profile pandarouter

/root/.hermes/profiles/pandarouter

VoIP route management and carrier research

Table 2. Telegram Hermes profiles.

The actor configured four additional profiles (dev, check, vuln, deploy) in a shared Telegram group. While we did not observe any chat artifacts for these profiles, the naming suggests the actor used AI to assist with development, validation, vulnerability testing and deployment automation functions.

The Cursor IDE was configured through a proxy script named cipher-proxy.sh that set environment variables to enable full agent mode and bypass its permission and sandbox controls. The configuration and the AI-generated scripts on the host shown below in Figure 7 suggest the actor used it for code development.

Attribution

We assess the actor is a financially motivated, multi-domain criminal operator with no prior reporting. The actor is English-speaking with informal, frequently broken grammar. The alice bot's stored memory describes the actor as a “gamer, OSINT, VoIP entrepreneur” claiming to hold a US LLC and EIN. Figure 8 below shows text from the pandarouter bot's stored memory, which is more candid.

Table 3 lists further attribution indicators of this actor.

Indicator

Value

Email

bugstergap@gmail.com

Display name

B U G S T E R

Cursor IDE user ID

158034011

Telegram user ID

7593151260

Table 3. Attribution indicators.

Conclusion

This case illustrates how AI lowers the skill barrier for cybercrime. The actor used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, but still achieved notable impact. They recovered more than 5,200 PII records and mapped multiple organizations' attack surfaces. AI enabled a single actor to operate across diverse attack types (credential theft, VoIP fraud, Wi-Fi cracking, cryptocurrency targeting) that would traditionally require distinct skill sets.

The VoIP fraud planning demonstrates a particularly notable use of AI as a domain expert. With DeepSeek V4 as the underlying model, the actor's bot profiles provided detailed, actionable criminal guidance.

This guidance included specific fraud-to-clean traffic ratios, carrier audit thresholds to stay below and operational security measures to avoid detection. The model's minimal safety controls allowed it to function as an on-demand criminal advisor, enabling the actor to acquire operational expertise through conversation rather than experience.

Combining these findings with our previous reporting on a Chinese-Speaking threat actor leveraging the Hermes + DeepSeek toolchain points to growing uptake of this combination among cybercriminals.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products:

By embedding the functional identity baselines discussed in this research into our detection engine for both cloud VM compute and serverless agents, Cortex Cloud adds a vital layer of operational context, enabling security teams to filter out noisy false positives and decisively catch threat actors attempting to disguise their presence, alter configurations or execute anomalous operations in the environment.

Idira Secrets Manager is designed to help secure and automate API keys and webhook tokens just-in-time to eliminate hardcoded credentials and prevent exfiltration.
